parts.name: Resistor
parts.what: Small cylinders with coloured bands (through-hole), or black chips marked with a number code like 103 (10kΩ) or 4701 (4.7kΩ).
fails: Goes open (infinite resistance) or high after overheating: often looks burnt or cracked.
Rarely shorts. High-value resistors (over 100kΩ) in power supplies drift high with age.

do: Lift one leg (or remove it) so nothing else is in parallel.
Meter on resistance (Ω). Touch the probes to each end, keeping fingers off the metal.
tests.good: Within its tolerance of the marked value (usually 1% or 5%).
tests.bad: Open (OL), or far from the marked value.

do: Power off, capacitors discharged. Measure across it in place.
tests.good: Equal to or lower than the marked value (other parts in parallel can only lower it).
tests.bad: Higher than the marked value: it's definitely faulty.

parts.replace: Same value, same power rating or higher (size is a clue: 1/4W is about 6mm long), same tolerance.
parts.salvage: Not worth it: resistors are cheap. Keep a kit instead.

parts.name: Potentiometer or trimmer
parts.what: A knob or slider (volume, tone), or a small trimmer adjusted with a screwdriver. Three pins: two ends and the wiper.
fails: Dirty or worn track: crackles, jumps or dead spots as it turns.
Open track: no change over part of its travel.

do: Power off. Meter on resistance between the middle pin and one end.
Turn it slowly from one end to the other while watching the reading.
tests.good: The reading changes smoothly from near 0 to the full value.
tests.bad: Jumps, flickers to OL, or doesn't change.

app.how: Meterie's graph shows a jump or dead spot as you turn it much better than the display can.

parts.replace: Same value and taper (a letter: A is log for volume, B is linear), same shaft and pin spacing. Try contact cleaner first.
parts.salvage: Yes, if they're smooth: knobs, pots and switches from old audio gear are useful.

parts.name: Electrolytic capacitor
parts.what: A can with a stripe marking the negative leg, rated in µF and volts. Common in power supplies and audio.
fails: Dries out with age and heat: capacitance drops and ESR rises, often with no visible sign.
Bulges at the top, leaks brown crust, or vents. Can short.

do: Tops should be flat, with no crust on the board under them.
tests.good: Flat top, clean base.
tests.bad: Domed top, crust, or pushed up off the board.

do: Discharge it, then measure with an ESR meter or component tester.
tests.good: ESR at or below the chart for its µF and voltage (often under 1Ω for 100µF+).
tests.bad: ESR several times the chart value, even if the µF reads fine.

do: Discharge it. Meter on capacitance, red probe to the + leg.
tests.good: Within about 20% of the marked value.
tests.bad: Well below the marked value, or reading as a short.

parts.replace: Same µF, the same or higher voltage, 105°C, and low-ESR in power supplies. Fit it the right way round.
parts.salvage: No: old electrolytics are the part most likely to fail. Replace rather than reuse.

parts.name: Ceramic or film capacitor
parts.what: Small beige or brown chips (surface-mount), or blue/yellow blobs and boxes. Used for decoupling and filtering.
fails: Tiny ceramic chips crack and short, pulling a power rail down: the most common cause of a shorted rail.
Film capacitors across the mains (X2) crack and burn with age.

do: Power off. Resistance across it: a short reads near 0Ω, but so does everything else on that rail.
If the rail is shorted, inject a little current into it (see Board level: find the short): the shorted capacitor gets warm.
tests.good: Not shorted, and stays cool when current is injected.
tests.bad: Short, and the warm spot is on it.

parts.replace: Same capacitance and voltage or higher; for X2 or Y capacitors across the mains, only the same safety rating.

parts.name: Diode
parts.what: A small cylinder with a band at one end (the cathode), or a surface-mount part marked with a line.
fails: Shorts (reads close to 0V both ways), especially rectifiers after a surge.
Goes open (OL both ways). Schottky diodes leak when hot.

tests.t: Diode test (in or out of the circuit, power off)
do: Meter on diode test. Red probe on the end without the band, black on the band.
Then swap the probes.
tests.good: About 0.5–0.7V one way (0.15–0.4V for Schottky), OL the other way.
tests.bad: Close to 0V both ways (shorted) or OL both ways (open).

parts.replace: Same type (rectifier, fast, Schottky, signal) with the same or higher current and voltage rating.

parts.name: Zener diode
parts.what: Looks like a diode, but sets a voltage: marked with it (like 5V1, or a code).
fails: Shorts after being overloaded; or the voltage drifts.

do: As for a diode: one way only should conduct.
tests.good: About 0.7V one way, OL the other (a meter can't show the zener voltage).
tests.bad: Shorted both ways.

do: Measure across it with the circuit running.
tests.good: Close to its marked voltage.
tests.bad: Far from it, or 0V.

parts.replace: Same voltage and power rating.

parts.name: LED
parts.what: Light-emitting diode: the longer leg (or the side without the flat) is +.
fails: Goes open, dims, or one colour of an RGB LED dies. In strips, one dead LED can stop the rest.

do: Meter on diode test, red to + (the longer leg). Many meters light the LED faintly.
tests.good: It glows faintly, or reads about 1.6–3.2V one way.
tests.bad: OL both ways, or no glow with a meter that lights others.

parts.replace: Same colour, size and forward voltage. Keep the resistor that sets its current.
parts.salvage: Yes: through-hole LEDs from old boards are fine to reuse after a quick test.

parts.name: Bridge rectifier
parts.what: Four diodes in one block, marked ~ ~ + −, or four separate diodes in a square near a power input.
fails: One or more diodes short after a surge, blowing the fuse.

do: Diode test from each ~ pin to + (red on ~), and from − to each ~ (red on −).
Then reverse each one.
tests.good: About 0.5V forward on all four, OL in reverse.
tests.bad: Any one near 0V both ways (shorted).

parts.replace: Same current and voltage rating or higher.

parts.name: Transistor (BJT)
parts.what: Three-legged black part (TO-92) or a surface-mount chip marked with a code: NPN or PNP, pins collector, base, emitter.
fails: Collector-emitter short (the most common), or an open junction.

do: Find the pinout from its number (look it up; a component tester works it out for you).
NPN: red on base, black on collector, then on emitter: both about 0.6V. Reverse: OL. PNP: the same with black on the base.
Collector to emitter: OL both ways.
tests.good: Both base junctions about 0.5–0.7V one way and OL the other; collector-emitter OL.
tests.bad: Any junction near 0V, or collector-emitter shorted.

parts.replace: Same part number, or one with the same type (NPN/PNP), pinout, and at least the same voltage, current and gain.

parts.name: MOSFET
parts.what: A power transistor (TO-220, DPAK, or small SOT-23): pins gate, drain, source. Switches motors, heaters, LEDs and power supplies.
fails: Drain-source short (stuck on), often with a cracked case or a burnt mark.
Gate damaged by static or overvoltage.

tests.t: Diode test (out of the circuit is best)
do: Short all three legs briefly to discharge the gate.
N-channel: red on source, black on drain: about 0.4–0.7V (the built-in diode). Reverse: OL.
Gate to the other two: OL both ways.
To check it switches: touch red to gate and black to source for a moment, then measure drain-source again: it should now conduct.
tests.good: Body diode reads normally, no short, gate OL, and it switches on when the gate is charged.
tests.bad: Drain-source near 0V both ways, or the gate isn't OL.

parts.replace: Same part, or with the same or higher voltage and current, the same or lower on-resistance, a logic-level gate if it's driven from a microcontroller, and the same pinout.

parts.name: Linear voltage regulator
parts.what: Three-legged part (78xx, LM1117, AMS1117, LM317) or small surface-mount chip turning a higher voltage into a fixed one.
fails: Output missing or wrong, overheating, or shorted input to output. Pinouts differ between types: wrong orientation is common in builds.

do: Look up the pinout from its number (78xx is IN-GND-OUT; AMS1117 is GND-OUT-IN).
Measure input to ground and output to ground with the circuit on.
tests.good: Input at least 1–2V above the output (less for LDOs), output at its rated voltage.
tests.bad: Input fine but output missing or low: the regulator, or something shorting the output. Unplug the load to tell which.

parts.replace: Same output voltage, pinout and current, and the same or lower dropout. Check the output capacitor the datasheet asks for.
parts.salvage: Yes: 78xx and LM317 regulators are worth keeping.

parts.name: Switching regulator (buck or boost)
parts.what: A chip with an inductor (a small coil, often a black block marked 4R7, 100…) and a diode nearby; turns one DC voltage into another efficiently.
fails: No output (failed chip, open inductor, enable pin held off), or output shorted.
Dried input or output capacitors make it whine, drop out or reset loads.

do: Input voltage present at the chip.
Enable (EN) pin high (above about 1.2V; check its datasheet).
Output at its rated voltage.
tests.good: All present and right.
tests.bad: Input present but no output, with enable high.

do: Scope probe on the pad between the chip and the inductor, ground clip short.
tests.good: A square wave of about the input voltage, at a few hundred kHz to a few MHz.
tests.bad: Flat line: the chip isn't switching.

app.how: Set the timebase to about 1µs/div and trigger on CH1's rising edge; turn on the Frequency and Peak-to-peak measurements.

parts.replace: Same chip; or a ready-made buck module of the right voltage and current as a bodge.
parts.salvage: Yes: buck and boost modules from dead gadgets are handy for projects.

parts.name: Crystal or resonator
parts.what: A metal can (HC-49), or a small surface-mount box, marked with its frequency (8.000, 16.000, 32.768…). Usually next to the processor with two small capacitors.
fails: Cracked by a drop; stops oscillating; or the circuit's capacitors fail. Without a clock, a processor does nothing.

do: Use a ×10 probe (×1 probes load it enough to stop it).
Probe the crystal's output pin (often marked XOUT, XTAL2 or OSC_OUT), not the input.
tests.good: A sine or rounded square wave at the marked frequency.
tests.bad: Flat line, or a frequency far from the marking.

app.how: ×10 probe, timebase so a few cycles fill the screen (about 50ns/div for 16MHz), AC or DC coupling, turn on Frequency.

parts.replace: Same frequency and type; keep the two load capacitors.

parts.name: Logic chip (74xx, 4000)
parts.what: Black chips with 14 or 16 pins and numbers like 74HC04, 74LS138, CD4017.
fails: Inputs or outputs damaged by static or overvoltage: an output stuck high or low.

do: Find the pinout in its datasheet. Check VCC (usually pin 14 or 16) and GND (pin 7 or 8).
Watch an input and the output it drives: does the output follow the logic it should?
tests.good: Power present, and outputs follow their inputs as the datasheet says.
tests.bad: An output stuck while its inputs change, or a chip that gets hot.

app.how: Clip one channel to each input and the output, capture, and compare: Probie shows which signals change together.

parts.replace: Same part number; the family letters matter (HC, HCT, LS have different input levels).
parts.salvage: Yes, in sockets: old 74xx and 4000 chips are useful for projects and learning.

parts.name: Microcontroller or processor
parts.what: The main chip that runs the device's program: an Atmel/Microchip, STM32, ESP, or a custom chip.
fails: Rarely the first thing to fail. Usually it's missing power, clock or reset, or its program (in flash) is corrupted.

do: Every power pin at the right voltage (VCC, VDD, VDDA, AVCC).
Clock running (see crystal).
Reset pin at its 'run' level (usually high).
Activity on its pins, or messages on its serial pins.
tests.good: Power, clock and reset all right, and pins toggling.
tests.bad: All three right but no activity at all: a corrupt program or a failed chip.

app.how: Capture the serial TX pin (Serial tab at 115200 first), or several I/O pins on the Logic tab to see whether it's doing anything.

parts.replace: Same chip, programmed with the device's firmware (from a backup or the maker): usually a job for the maker or a specialist.
parts.salvage: Development boards: yes. Chips soldered on old boards: rarely worth removing.

parts.name: Op-amp
parts.what: 8-pin chips like TL072, NE5532, LM358: in audio, sensor and filter circuits.
fails: Output stuck at one supply rail, or noisy. Audio op-amps fail after a supply fault.

do: Supply pins (often 8 and 4) at the expected voltages.
With no signal, outputs (pins 1 and 7 on dual op-amps) usually sit in the middle: 0V on a ± supply, half the supply on a single one.
tests.good: Outputs at their resting level, and a test tone passes through.
tests.bad: An output stuck at a supply rail.

app.how: Feed a test tone in and compare the input and output pins on CH1 and CH2.

parts.replace: Same part, or a pin-compatible op-amp that works on the same supply.

parts.name: Optocoupler
parts.what: A 4- or 6-pin chip (PC817 and similar) that passes a signal across an isolation gap with an LED and a sensor. In power supplies it carries the voltage feedback.
fails: The LED inside wears out: a power supply's output drifts high or it cycles.

do: Diode test across the LED pins (1 and 2): about 1.1V one way.
Light the LED through a 1kΩ resistor from 5V and measure the output pins (4 to 3) on resistance: it should drop sharply.
tests.good: LED conducts one way, and the output switches when the LED is lit.
tests.bad: LED open, or the output doesn't change.

parts.replace: Same part (the current transfer ratio matters in power supplies).

parts.name: Fuse or polyfuse
parts.what: Glass or ceramic tubes, small surface-mount fuses (marked F), or green/yellow polyfuses (resettable).
fails: Blows because something after it drew too much current. Polyfuses go high-resistance and recover when cool.

do: Meter on continuity or low ohms across it.
tests.good: A beep: under 1Ω (polyfuses: a few ohms at most).
tests.bad: OL: blown.

parts.replace: Same current, voltage and speed (fast or slow-blow). Never bigger. Find why it blew before powering up.

parts.name: Protection diode, TVS or varistor
parts.what: Small diodes or discs right at an input (USB, DC jack, mains) that clamp spikes.
fails: Shorts after a spike to protect everything else: the input then reads as a dead short.

do: Diode test or resistance across it. Lift one end if the reading could be something else.
tests.good: Not shorted (a TVS reads like a diode or OL).
tests.bad: Close to 0Ω both ways.

parts.replace: Same type and voltage. A device often still works with it removed, but put a new one in before using it for real.

parts.name: Relay
parts.what: A box (often blue or black) that clicks: a coil moves a switch. Pins: coil, common, normally open (NO), normally closed (NC).
fails: Coil open; contacts burnt, so they don't pass current even when they click; contacts welded shut.

do: Coil resistance: tens to hundreds of ohms (the rating is on the case).
Common to NC: should beep; common to NO: OL.
Power the coil at its rated voltage: it clicks and the two swap. Check the contacts carry current, not just beep.
tests.good: Coil reads normally, it clicks, and the contacts swap cleanly.
tests.bad: Coil OL, no click, or contacts that don't swap or stay closed.

parts.replace: Same coil voltage, the same or higher contact rating, same footprint.
parts.salvage: Yes: relays from old appliances and boards are handy, after a test.

parts.name: Switch or button
parts.what: Tactile buttons, slide and toggle switches, microswitches, keyboard switches.
fails: Dirty or worn contacts: works sometimes, or bounces. Broken internal spring.

do: Power off. Continuity across the switch (small 4-leg buttons: try across the corners).
tests.good: Beeps only while pressed, crisply.
tests.bad: Never beeps, beeps all the time, or crackles.

app.how: Meterie's continuity mode with the graph shows a crackly contact as a ragged line.

parts.replace: Same size and action; contact cleaner first.
parts.salvage: Yes: switches, buttons and keyboard switches are worth keeping.

parts.name: Connector, cable or ribbon
parts.what: Plugs and sockets, wire harnesses, and flat ribbon or flex cables.
fails: Broken wire inside the sheath, cracked flex cable, corroded or loose contacts, cracked solder joints on the socket.

do: Power off. Continuity from each pin at one end to the matching pin at the other.
Flex the cable while it beeps: the beep must not break.
Check neighbouring pins aren't joined.
tests.good: Every wire beeps, steadily, and no two are joined.
tests.bad: A wire that's OL or cuts in and out.

app.how: Meterie's continuity beep and graph catch a break that only opens when the cable bends.

parts.replace: Same connector type and pitch; ribbon cables by width, pitch and length.
parts.salvage: Yes: cables, connectors and ribbon cables are some of the most reusable parts.

parts.name: Speaker or buzzer
parts.what: Speakers (marked 4Ω or 8Ω), piezo buzzers and magnetic buzzers.
fails: Open voice coil, torn cone, rubbing coil (buzzes).

do: Unplug one wire. Meter on resistance.
tests.good: A speaker reads a bit under its marking (8Ω reads about 6–7.5Ω); a magnetic buzzer tens of ohms.
tests.bad: OL (open coil) or near 0.

parts.replace: Same impedance (Ω), same or higher power, and a size that fits.
parts.salvage: Yes: speakers from old TVs and toys are fine for projects.

parts.name: DC motor
parts.what: Small brushed motors in toys, fans, drives and tools.
fails: Worn brushes, open winding, seized bearing, a shorted winding that draws too much current.

do: Power off. Resistance across its terminals while turning it slowly by hand.
tests.good: A few ohms that stays fairly steady as it turns.
tests.bad: OL at some positions (worn brushes or a dead segment) or 0Ω (shorted).

do: Run it from a bench supply at its voltage and watch the current with no load.
tests.good: Small and steady current that drops once it's up to speed.
tests.bad: High current and little speed: a shorted winding or tight bearing.

parts.replace: Same voltage, size, shaft and speed.
parts.salvage: Yes: motors, gears and fans from old printers and toys are classic project parts.

parts.name: Lithium-ion cell (18650 and others)
parts.what: Cylindrical cells (18650, 21700) in laptop and tool packs, or flat pouch cells.
fails: Loses capacity with age; self-discharges when faulty; swells (pouch cells). A cell left below 2.5V can be damaged inside.

do: Measure each cell: 3.0–4.2V is the normal range.
Below 2.5V: don't charge it unless you have a charger with a recovery mode; below 1.5V, recycle it.
Charge fully, wait a week, and measure again: a cell that's dropped more than 0.1V self-discharges and must not be used.
A capacity tester shows what's left: below about 70% of its rating isn't worth keeping.
tests.good: 3.0–4.2V, holds its charge, and decent capacity.
tests.bad: Below 2.5V, a big drop over a week, swelling, or very low capacity.

bands.say: Over-discharged: only with a recovery charger, if at all.

parts.replace: Same chemistry and size, from a reputable maker; matched cells in packs.
parts.salvage: Yes, with care: good cells from laptop packs power many projects. Always use a protection board (BMS).

parts.name: LCD or display module
parts.what: Character LCDs (16×2), small graphic LCDs and OLEDs, LED segment displays.
fails: No backlight, missing segments or lines (connections), contrast set wrong, or a dead driver chip.

do: Power pins at the right voltage.
Character LCDs: turn the contrast trimmer slowly: a row of blocks should appear.
Backlight pins (A and K): about 3–4V across a working backlight.
Data pins: watch them while the device writes to the display.
tests.good: Blocks appear with contrast, backlight lights, data pins toggle.
tests.bad: Nothing with power and contrast right: the module; data pins quiet: the device isn't writing.

app.how: Capture the display's data or I2C/SPI pins to see whether the device is sending to it.

parts.replace: Same model; many character LCDs are interchangeable.
parts.salvage: Yes: displays from old gadgets are great for projects, after checking the pinout.

categories.name: Computer or laptop
categories.open: Laptops usually open from the bottom: remove every screw (some hide under rubber feet or stickers), then prise the base off with a plastic pick, and unplug the battery before touching the board. Desktop PCs: the side panel comes off, but never open the power supply box itself.

categories.name: Phone or tablet
categories.open: Phones and tablets are glued shut. Warm the edge to about 80°C (a hair dryer or heat pad), lift with a suction cup and slide plastic picks round. Disconnect the battery connector first, before anything else.

categories.name: Games console or controller
categories.open: Consoles and controllers use security screws (often Torx or tri-point), some under stickers or grips, then clips. Unplug the battery in controllers first; a console's built-in power supply holds mains voltage.

categories.name: TV, monitor or display
categories.open: Lay it face down on something soft. The back comes off with screws and clips. The power board holds mains voltage and big capacitors: unplug it and leave it a few minutes before touching anything.

categories.name: Speaker, headphones, amp or radio
categories.open: Small speakers and earbuds are usually glued or welded: prise the seam gently with a thin plastic pick and mind the battery wires. Amplifiers have big capacitors that stay charged after unplugging.

categories.name: Toy or gadget
categories.open: Usually small Phillips screws: check under the battery cover and stickers. Some snap apart with a plastic pick round the seam.

categories.name: Cordless tool or battery pack
categories.open: Screws round the body. Battery packs hold a lot of energy even when 'flat': never short the terminals, and keep them away from metal tools.

categories.name: Lights and LEDs
categories.open: LED strips need no opening. Lamps with a built-in driver run from the mains: unplug first.

categories.name: Electronics project or board
categories.open: Nothing to open: unplug USB and anything else powering it before changing wiring.

categories.name: Keyboard, mouse or remote
categories.open: Keycaps pull off with a keycap puller. Mice have screws under the gliding pads; remotes snap apart at the seam.

categories.name: 3D printer or machine with motors
categories.open: Switch off and unplug at the wall. The power supply has mains terminals, often with no cover: keep fingers and tools away from them.

categories.name: Household gadget (fan, vacuum, shaver…)
categories.open: Screws, often hidden under feet or labels. Unplug before opening; mains motors are wired straight to the mains.

danger.why: A microwave's high-voltage capacitor can hold a lethal charge long after it's unplugged, and its magnetron runs at over 2000 volts.

danger.t: Anything that heats from the mains
danger.why: Ovens, toasters, kettles, heaters, irons and the like pass large mains currents through bare elements. A mistake can mean a fatal shock or a house fire.
Washing machines, dishwashers, dryers, fridges and freezers combine mains power with water, heavy moving parts or pressurised refrigerant.
These store or make thousands of volts: enough to kill, even when switched off.

danger.t: Anything wired into the house, or gas
danger.why: Fixed wiring and gas work must be done by a qualified electrician or gas engineer, by law in many countries.
E-bike, scooter and car batteries hold enough energy to start fires that are very hard to put out; car and mobility batteries can explode or leak acid.
If one of these fails after a home repair, someone could be hurt. They must be repaired or replaced by the maker.

symptoms.desc: No lights, no sound, nothing happens.

symptoms.desc: Starts, then cuts out, keeps rebooting, or switches off under load.

symptoms.name: Won't charge, or the battery runs out fast
symptoms.desc: The charging light or icon doesn't come on, or it's flat in no time.

symptoms.name: No picture, or the screen is dim, lined or garbled
symptoms.desc: It sounds or feels like it's on, but the screen is wrong.

symptoms.name: No sound, or it hums, crackles or distorts
symptoms.desc: Speakers silent, one side out, or sound is noisy.

symptoms.name: Buttons, keys or touch don't respond
symptoms.desc: Something you press doesn't do anything, or does the wrong thing.

symptoms.name: A motor or fan won't spin, or is noisy
Its heater doesn't heat, or won't stop
symptoms.desc: A 3D printer hot end or bed stays cold, overheats, or shows a heating error.

symptoms.name: Won't connect: USB, Wi-Fi or Bluetooth
symptoms.desc: The computer doesn't see it, or it won't pair.

symptoms.name: The computer can't see the board, or code won't upload
symptoms.desc: No COM port, upload errors, or it won't run your code.

symptoms.name: LEDs flicker, part is out, or colours are wrong
symptoms.desc: Some LEDs dark, wrong colours, dim at one end.

symptoms.name: Gets hot, smells of burning, or smoked
symptoms.desc: Too hot to touch, a burning smell, smoke or a bang.

symptoms.name: Got wet, or had a drink spilled on it
symptoms.desc: Rain, a spill, dropped in water, or condensation.

symptoms.name: Works sometimes, cuts out when moved
symptoms.desc: Comes and goes, works when you hold the cable just so.

symptoms.name: Trips the electricity or blows its fuse
symptoms.desc: The house breaker or RCD trips, or the plug fuse blows.

dead.1.why: Most 'dead' devices aren't: whatever powers them is the problem far more often than the device itself.

do.t: Plug it into a different wall socket that you know works (try a lamp in it first). Skip extension leads for now.
Try a different adapter with the same voltage, plug and polarity, if you have one.
Try a different USB charger and cable that you know work with another device.
Try a different charger that you know works.
Try a different battery pack that you know is charged, and charge this pack on its charger: the charger's light shows whether it's taking charge.
Try a different USB port, ideally one on the back of a computer or a USB wall charger rather than a hub.
Put in fresh batteries, checking each one faces the right way (+ to +).
Leave it on the charger for at least 30 minutes: a completely flat battery may show nothing at first.

dead.1.q: Does it come to life with power you know is good?
dead.1.good: It powers up, so the device is fine and the supply was the problem.

dead.2.t: Check the batteries and their contacts
dead.2.why: Leaking batteries leave a crust that stops the current, and springs lose their grip.
do: Take the batteries out and look at the springs and contacts with a torch.
Green, blue or white crust is corrosion from a leaking battery.
Measure each battery with a multimeter on DC volts (the 20V range, or auto). A fresh AA or AAA reads about 1.5–1.6V; under 1.2V is flat.
dead.2.q: Were the contacts crusty, or the batteries flat?

a.t: No, they look clean and the batteries are good

dead.2.good: Shiny metal contacts, firm springs, and each cell above 1.3V.
dead.2.bad: Crust on the contacts, a weak spring, or a cell below 1.2V.

dead.pack.why: Tool packs have protection that switches the pack off when it's run right down or a cell is faulty.
do: Set the multimeter to DC volts and measure across the pack's main + and − terminals.
An 18V (20V max) pack reads about 18–20.5V charged, and about 15–16V flat. 12V packs: about 10.5–12.5V. 36V packs: about 32–41V.
A pack that reads 0V or very low has shut itself off: try it on its charger; some chargers can't wake a pack that's gone too low.
dead.pack.good: Within the range for its voltage.

dead.3.t: Measure what the charger or adapter gives out
dead.3.why: A dead adapter looks exactly like a dead device. Measuring it takes a minute.
do: Read the label on the adapter: it says what it should give out, such as 'Output: 12V ⎓ 2A' or '5V 3A'.

do.t: Set the multimeter to DC volts. For a round barrel plug, put one probe inside the hole (centre pin) and the other on the outside sleeve. The small symbol on the label shows which is + (usually the centre).
For USB, plug a USB power meter between the charger and the device: it shows the voltage and the current. Without one, use a USB breakout board.

do: An adapter with nothing plugged in can read up to about 10% high: that's normal.
dead.3.q: Is the output close to what the label says?

a.t: No: nothing, much lower, or jumping about

dead.3.good: Within about 10% of the label (5V: 4.75–5.25V; 12V: about 11–13V).
dead.3.bad: 0V, far too low, or a reading that keeps changing.

dead.3b.t: Watch whether it takes any current
dead.3b.why: A device that draws current is getting power and doing something with it. One that draws nothing isn't connected.
do: With the USB power meter (or a bench power supply's current reading) in line, plug the device in and watch the current (A) for a minute.

do.t: Then try a forced restart: on an iPhone press volume up, volume down, then hold the side button for 15 seconds; on most Android phones hold power and volume down for 20 seconds.
Then unplug the charger and hold the power button for 30 seconds, and try again. Some laptops have a small battery-reset hole underneath.
Then hold the power button for 15–30 seconds; some gadgets also have a small reset hole.
Then look for a small reset hole, and press it with a paper clip.

dead.port.why: Lint and dirt build up in ports until the plug can't reach the contacts, and sockets work loose.
do: Shine a torch into the port and look with a magnifier or your phone's camera zoomed in.
Scrape out lint with a wooden toothpick or a plastic pick. Never use metal: the pins short easily.
Check the plug clicks firmly home and doesn't wobble. Look for bent or missing pins.

a.t: Lint or dirt came out, and it works now
The port wobbles or pins are damaged
The port is clean and solid

dead.flat.why: Lithium batteries that have gone below their safe voltage charge very slowly at first, and some devices show nothing until they've recovered.
do: Leave it on its own charger for an hour.
Then do the forced restart again.

dead.4.t: Check the switch, and any fuse or lead
dead.4.why: These are the simplest parts on the power path, and the most likely to fail.

do.t: Unplug it. In the UK, plugs have a fuse: open the plug (or the fuse drawer) and test the fuse with the multimeter on continuity (the beep setting). A beep means it's good; no beep means it's blown.
Check the lead along its length, especially where it goes into the plug and the device: cuts, kinks, scorch marks or a loose cord grip.
Unplugged, test each wire of the lead end to end on continuity, bending the lead as you go. The beep should stay steady.

do: Make sure the on/off switch clicks and, if you can reach its contacts, that it beeps on continuity when switched on.
dead.4.good: The fuse and each wire beep steadily (close to 0Ω).
dead.4.bad: No beep (OL on the meter), or a beep that cuts in and out as you bend the lead.

dead.fuse.why: A fuse blows for a reason. If a new one blows straight away, something inside is shorted and must be found first.
do: Fit a new fuse of exactly the same rating (it's printed on it: 3A, 5A, 13A…). Never fit a bigger fuse, and never bridge it with wire or foil.
Plug in and switch on.

dead.5.t: Open it up and look inside
dead.5.why: Faults that kill a device usually leave marks you can see: burnt parts, bulging capacitors or corrosion.
do: Take a photo before every step, and keep screws in order (an ice-cube tray or a magnetic mat works well).

do.t: Disconnect the battery first: lever its connector straight up with a plastic tool.
Wait a few minutes after unplugging, then check the big capacitors are discharged (see Safety) before touching anything.

do: Look over every part of the board under a bright light, with a magnifier. Sniff too: burnt parts have a sharp smell.

dead.6.why: Devices that run from the mains have a fuse on the power board, near where the mains comes in.
do: Unplugged. Find the fuse near the mains input: a glass tube or a small ceramic or black part marked F1 (or F with a number).
Test it on continuity.
dead.6.bad: No beep, or the glass is blackened inside.

dead.7.why: Boards turn the input into a few fixed voltages ('rails'), such as 5V, 3.3V and 1.8V. A missing rail points straight at the fault.
do: Find test points or parts marked 5V, 3V3, VCC or VBAT, or the regulators (small 3- or 5-legged parts near the power input). A board diagram or service manual helps a lot.
Put the black probe on ground: a metal shield, the metal shell of a socket, or a screw hole.

do.t: Never use the mains side of a power supply as ground: that 'ground' is live.
On a PC power supply you can check it on its own: link the green wire to a black one on the 24-pin plug and it starts. Yellow should be 12V, red 5V, orange 3.3V, purple 5V standby.

do: Switch on and measure each rail with the red probe. Keep one hand away from the board.

a.t: One is missing or much too low
Nothing at all from the supply

dead.7.good: Each rail within about 5% of its value.
dead.7.bad: 0V, or a rail that's well below what it should be (pulled down by a short).

dead.8.why: A rail that's missing or pulled low is often shorted to ground by one failed part, which gets warm when power goes into it.
do: Unplug. Measure the resistance from the rail to ground. Under about 5Ω usually means a short (a busy rail with a big chip can read 10–100Ω: compare with a similar board if you can).
Feed the rail from a bench power supply set to its voltage, with the current limit low (start at 0.5A). The shorted part warms up.
Find the warm part: a thermal camera, a drop of isopropyl alcohol that evaporates first, freeze spray that melts first, or carefully with a fingertip.
The usual suspects: tiny ceramic capacitors, protection diodes, and regulators.
dead.8.q: Did you find a part that heats up?

a.t: It's shorted, but nothing warms up

dead.9.why: With power present, the next step is whether it's being told to start.

do.t: Test the power button on continuity: it should beep only while pressed.
Development boards: press reset, and check the power LED. An on-board LED that blinks shows its code is running.
Check anything that switches it on (a switch, a sensor, a remote) is working.
On a desktop, short the two 'PWR SW' pins on the motherboard with a screwdriver tip to bypass the case button.
Take out all but one memory stick, unplug extra drives and cards, and clear the BIOS settings (the CMOS jumper or the coin battery out for a minute).
Unplug the battery inside and try on the charger alone; take out and refit the memory if it isn't soldered in.

do: Listen for beeps and watch for blinking lights: they're often a code for the fault.

a.t: The power switch doesn't close when pressed
It started once the switch was bypassed
It started after reseating the memory or cards
It beeps or flashes a pattern

so.1.t: Notice exactly when it switches off
so.1.why: When it cuts out says a lot about why.
do: Use it until it cuts out, a few times, and notice what's happening each time.

a.t: On battery, but fine on the charger
Once the batteries aren't brand new
After it's been on a while, or when warm
When it's working hard (busy, heavy load, loud)
Straight away, a second after starting

so.2.why: Chips switch themselves off to protect themselves when they overheat. Dust and dried thermal paste are the usual reasons.
do: Check the fan spins when it's on, and air comes out of the vents.
Look into the vents with a torch: grey felt across the heatsink fins blocks the air completely.

do.t: Free tools like HWMonitor (Windows) show the temperatures. Over about 95°C for a processor is too hot.
Thermal paste dries out after four or five years.
3D printers: check the power supply's and mainboard's fans spin and their vents are clear; a hot mainboard's stepper drivers shut down.

a.t: It's clean and the fan works

so.3.t: Check the power holds up under load
so.3.why: A tired or undersized power source can't keep up when the device works hard.

do.t: Measure the supply while it's working hard: a USB power meter in line shows the voltage dropping.
Measure the battery while it's working hard, with the meter across its terminals.
Measure the power supply's low-voltage output on the board while it's working hard: never the mains side.
Measure the power input on the board while it's working hard.
Check the adapter's watts match the one it came with. A lower-power adapter makes laptops shut off or slow down.
Check the power supply's watts are enough for the graphics card (its maker says what's recommended).

so.3.q: Does the voltage drop a lot when it's working?

so.4.why: These two are the classic reasons for a start-and-stop loop.

do.t: Disconnect the battery and look at it: it should be completely flat. Puffy, bent or rounded means swollen.

do: Look at the round capacitors on the board: their tops should be flat. Domed or leaking tops mean they've failed.

ch.1.why: Cables fail far more often than devices. A cheap or worn cable may charge some devices and not others.

do.t: Try a different cable, and a different charger, that you know work.
If it can charge on a charging pad, try that: if the pad works and the cable doesn't, the port is the problem.
Try the pack on another charger, and another pack on this charger. A flashing fault light on the charger usually means the pack is too hot, too cold, or faulty.

a.t: It charges with another charger, cable or pack
The pad works, the cable doesn't

ch.2.why: How much current it takes tells you which part of the charging path has stopped.
do: Plug a USB power meter between the charger and the device and watch the current for a minute.
Normal charging is usually 0.5–3A, slowing right down near full.

a.t: 0.3 A or more, but the battery doesn't fill

bands.say: It's charging at a normal rate.

ch.3.why: A worn port makes poor contact, so it only charges slowly, or only at an angle.
do: Clean the port as in the port step (wooden toothpick, torch, no metal).
Gently hold the plug at different angles while watching the current.

a.t: Lint came out and it charges now
It charges only at an angle

ch.4.why: Batteries wear out: after a few hundred charges they hold much less.

do.t: iPhone: Settings, Battery, Battery Health. Android: many phones show it under Settings, Battery or Device care, or use an app like AccuBattery.
Windows: run 'powercfg /batteryreport' in a command prompt and compare 'Design capacity' with 'Full charge capacity'. macOS: System Information, Power, shows the cycle count and condition.
Measure the pack's voltage: an 18V pack reads about 18–20.5V when charged. Packs that read very low (under about 14V) may have shut themselves off; one weak cell group is common.
Look at the battery itself: any puffiness at all means it's swollen.

a.t: Worn: much less than it should hold

ch.5.why: If the battery is fine and power reaches the device, the charging chip or its battery sensor is next.

do.t: Measure the voltage on the battery's connector while it's charging: a single lithium cell slowly rises towards 4.2V (some to 4.35V).
Many batteries have a third wire for a temperature sensor. If it's broken or missing, the charger refuses to charge.

Measure the pack's voltage while it's on the charger: it should rise steadily. Chargers read the pack's temperature and cells through the small contacts between the main terminals: clean them and check none are bent.

ch.5.q: Does the battery voltage rise while charging?

dp.1.t: Is it the screen, or what feeds it?
dp.1.why: First find out whether the device is running and only the screen is out.

do.t: Connect another monitor or TV by HDMI or DisplayPort.
3D printers: check the printer still moves and heats when you send it a job from a computer or SD card: if it does, only the screen is out.
Ring it from another phone, or plug it into a computer: if it rings, vibrates or shows up, it's on.
Press Input or Source and try every input, and try a different HDMI cable and port. Check the TV's menu appears with nothing plugged in.

do: Listen for sounds and watch for lights that show it's running.

a.t: It works on another screen, or is clearly on

dp.2.t: Shine a torch at the screen
dp.2.why: LCD screens need a backlight. If only the backlight is out, the picture is still there, just in the dark.
do: With it on, shine a bright torch at the screen from close up, at an angle, in a dark room.

a.t: A picture with lines, blotches or wrong colours

dp.2.good: Nothing faint means the backlight isn't the (only) problem.
dp.2.bad: A faint picture under the torch means the backlight has failed.

dp.3.why: Backlights fail on their own: one dead LED can put out a whole row, and many boards have a small backlight fuse.

do.t: TVs: the LEDs are strips behind the panel. Lift the panel out carefully (it's fragile) and test each LED with an LED tester, or a meter's diode test (it may only glow faintly).
Look for a small fuse near the display connector on the board, and check it on continuity.
Burnt spots on the LEDs' lenses show the failed ones.
Small screens have their backlight in the screen module itself: check its cable and the backlight supply pins (often marked LED+ and LED−, or BL) on the board.

dp.3.q: Did you find a dead LED or a blown fuse?

dp.4.why: Display cables are thin and come loose after a knock.

do.t: Disconnect the battery first.
3D printer screens join the mainboard by one or two ribbon cables (often EXP1 and EXP2): check both are pushed fully home, the right way round and in the right sockets.

do: Find the display connector, open its latch (a flip-up bar or a sliding lock), pull the cable out, look at the contacts and refit it straight and fully home.
Look along the cable for creases, tears or burn marks.

dp.5.why: The shape of a screen fault tells you which part has failed.
do: Press gently along the edges of the screen and see if lines change.

a.t: Lines change when I press the edge
Cracks, ink blots or spreading patches
Half the screen or all the colours are wrong (TV)

dp.6.why: No picture anywhere means the computer isn't finishing its start-up.
do: Listen for beeps and watch the lights for a pattern.

do.t: Reseat the memory and the graphics card. Try one memory stick at a time, in the slot the motherboard's manual says.
Reseat the memory if it's not soldered in.

do: Clear the BIOS settings (the CMOS jumper, or take the coin battery out for a minute).

a.t: It beeps or flashes a pattern

snd.1.why: Most sound faults are a setting, or a cable.
do: Check the volume and mute, and that the right output is chosen (many devices switch outputs on their own).

do.t: Turn Bluetooth off on your other phones, tablets and computers nearby: it may be connected to one of them.

do: Try a different source and cable.
If it has a headphone socket, plug headphones in and out a few times: a stuck switch inside it mutes the speakers.

snd.2.why: Speakers fail on their own: the fine coil wire breaks, or the cone tears.
do: If it has a headphone socket and headphones work but the speaker doesn't, it's the speaker or its wiring.
Unplug or unsolder one speaker wire, then measure the speaker's resistance. A '4Ω' or '8Ω' speaker reads a bit less, about 3–7Ω.
Push the cone very gently: it should move smoothly with no scraping.

a.t: A few ohms: it looks fine

snd.3.why: Each noise has a usual cause.
do: Listen with the volume low and turn it up slowly. Move the knobs and switches.

a.t: Crackles when I move a knob or switch
Silence on one or both sides

snd.4.t: Follow the sound through the circuit
snd.4.why: Find the last point where the sound is still there.
do: With it on and the volume halfway, touch the input of the amplifier chip or stage with a screwdriver tip held by its handle: a hum in the speaker means everything from there on works.
With an oscilloscope (Scopie), follow a test tone from the input to the output and see where it stops.
Measure the amplifier chip's supply pins.

do.t: Amplifiers have a protection relay that clicks on a few seconds after switching on. If it clicks off again, the output has a fault.

a.t: A hum appears when I touch the amp's input
No hum even at the amplifier

bt.1.why: Dirt, sticky drinks and skin oil stop buttons making contact.
do: Switch it off and disconnect its power.

do.t: Take out the batteries.
For a keyboard, pull off the keycap with a keycap puller.

do: Clean round the button with isopropyl alcohol on a cotton bud, and blow out crumbs.
Press the button 20–30 times to work the cleaner in, then let it dry for 10 minutes.

do.t: Many devices have a hardware test in their diagnostics or a test app: use it to see whether the button registers at all.

bt.2.why: Touch problems are often dirt, a cover over the surface, the power supply or the software.

do.t: Take off the case and screen protector, clean the screen, and restart.
Clean the touch surface, take off any cover or sticker over it, and restart.
Try it with the charger unplugged: a poor charger can make touch go wild.
If the screen was replaced recently, cheap replacements often have poor touch.

a.t: It only misbehaves on the charger
Touch is still dead or jumpy

bt.3.t: Test the switch with a meter
bt.3.why: Find out whether the switch itself closes.
do: With all power disconnected, put the meter on continuity across the switch's legs.
It should beep only while you press it. Small square 4-leg switches have their legs joined in pairs, so try across corners.
bt.3.q: Does it beep when pressed, and not when released?

a.t: No, or it beeps all the time

bt.4.why: If the switch is fine, the connection from it is broken.
do: Follow the copper track or flex cable from the switch towards the chip, testing continuity along it.
Look closely for a cracked track, corrosion or a torn flex cable.

m.1.why: A motor that can't turn freely can't start, and may hum or blow its fuse.
do: Unplug it. Turn the shaft, blades or wheel by hand.
Feel for stiffness and grinding, and look for hair, string or fluff wound round the shaft.

m.2.why: Find out whether it's the motor, or what drives it.

do.t: Cooling fans: measure across the fan plug's red and black wires (usually 12V or 5V) while the device is on.
Low-voltage motors: measure across the motor's two terminals with its switch on.
Measure across the motor's two terminals with the trigger pressed.
Mains motors: only measure live if you're trained in mains work. Otherwise answer 'No power' and test the switch unplugged.
3D printer motors are driven by the mainboard: move the axis from the printer's menu and feel whether the motor locks (holds firm) when the printer is on.

m.3.why: Brushes wear down, windings break, and fans need their start capacitor.

do.t: Unplugged, measure the resistance across the motor: a few ohms is normal. Open (OL) means a broken winding or worn brushes.

Stepper motors: unplug the motor and measure across each pair of wires: two pairs read a few ohms (the two coils); open means a broken coil. Swap it with another axis's motor to see whether the fault moves.
Drills, blenders, vacuums and mixers have two carbon brushes, often behind round caps. Under about 5mm long, they're worn out.
Pedestal and ceiling fans that hum but don't spin need a new start capacitor (a small box marked µF).
For a cooling fan, try a spare fan of the same size and voltage.

a.t: The motor's fine: the fault moved with the driver

m.4.why: Something before the motor has stopped passing power.

do.t: Unplugged, test the on/off switch and each speed setting on continuity.
Mains motors often have a thermal fuse or cut-out taped into the windings. It should beep.
Cooling fans: check the fan's plug is fully on its header, and that the fan isn't turned off in the device's settings.
On a computer, check the fan isn't set to off or 0% in the BIOS fan settings.
3D printers: check the motor's cable at both ends and the end-stop switches; a stepper driver that's failed or too hot stops its motor.
Trigger switches in cordless tools wear out: test the trigger at full press.

h.1.why: Heaters are watched by safety checks that stop them when something isn't right.

do.t: 3D printers show an error (thermal runaway, MINTEMP, MAXTEMP, heating failed). Note exactly what it says.

do: Check the heater's and sensor's plugs are pushed fully home and not scorched.

h.2.why: The element is just a wire with a known resistance, so a meter tells you if it's broken.
do: Switch off, unplug the heater's wires from the board, and measure across them.
The expected resistance is the voltage squared divided by the power: a 24V 40W heater is 24×24÷40 ≈ 14Ω. Fixie works it out below.
Also measure from each terminal to the metal block or frame: that must read open (OL).

a.t: A low reading to the metal block

h.3.why: The heater is fine, so either the board isn't switching it on or the connection to it is bad.
do: Plug the heater back in and set it to heat.
Measure across the heater's terminals on the board: it should show the supply voltage (often 12V or 24V) while heating.
Look at the board's heater fuse (a small blade or surface-mount fuse near the power input) and check it on continuity, switched off.

a.t: Full voltage, but the heater stays cold
No voltage at the heater terminals
A blown fuse on the board

h.4.why: 3D printer errors say exactly which part of the heating loop has failed.
do: MINTEMP means the temperature sensor reads impossibly cold: an open sensor wire. MAXTEMP means impossibly hot: a shorted sensor.
A common sensor is a 100k thermistor: unplug it and measure about 100kΩ at room temperature (it falls as it warms).
'Heating failed' or 'thermal runaway' means it didn't heat as expected: a loose sensor or a failing heater.

do.t: A cooling fan pointed at the nozzle can cause it too: fit a fan duct or a silicone sock.

do: Check the crimped connectors on the heater and sensor wires: they work loose and burn.

cn.0.why: USB and wireless faults have different causes.
do: Think about which connection is failing.

cn.1.t: Try another cable, port and computer
cn.1.why: Many USB cables only carry power, with no data wires inside.
do: Use a cable you know transfers data (one you've used to copy files with).
Try a different port, directly on the computer rather than a hub, and if you can, a different computer.

cn.2.t: See whether the computer notices it at all
cn.2.why: Whether it appears, and how, points to the cause.
do: Windows: open Device Manager and plug it in. Watch for something new appearing, or an 'Unknown USB device' with a yellow mark.
Mac: System Information, USB. Linux: run 'lsusb', or 'sudo dmesg -w' and plug it in.

a.t: It appears with an error (like 'device descriptor request failed')
It appears, but the app can't use it

cn.3.why: Pairing gets muddled, and antenna leads come loose.
do: Forget the device on both sides and pair again. Switch both off and on.
Move closer, away from microwaves and other 2.4GHz gadgets.

do.t: Inside, Wi-Fi cards have small antenna leads that snap onto the card: they pop off after a repair.

a.t: I found a loose antenna lead

up.1.t: Use a data cable, and look for the port
up.1.why: The commonest cause by far is a charge-only USB cable.
do: Use a cable you know transfers data.
Plug the board in and look in Device Manager (Windows), System Information (Mac) or 'ls /dev/tty*' (Linux) for a new COM or serial port.
Flashie and Probie list the ports too.

up.2.t: Check the driver and the board's power
up.2.why: Cheaper boards use a USB-serial chip that needs a driver on some computers.
do: Look at the small chip near the USB socket: CH340, CP2102 or FT232 each have a free driver from their maker.
Boards with USB built into the main chip (Pico, ESP32-S3, Pro Micro) need no driver.
Check the power LED. If it's off, measure 5V and 3.3V on the board's pins.

a.t: The LED is on, but there's still no port

up.3.why: Boards need to be in a special mode to accept new code. Most switch on their own, but not always.
do: ESP32: hold BOOT, tap EN (or RST), let go of BOOT, then upload.
Raspberry Pi Pico: hold BOOTSEL while plugging it in: a drive called RPI-RP2 appears. Drag a .uf2 file onto it, or use Flashie.
Pro Micro and Leonardo: tap reset twice quickly, then upload within 8 seconds.
Close anything else using the port (a serial monitor, Probie, Cura).
Check the right board and port are chosen in your software.

up.4.t: Check what's wired to the pins
up.4.why: Some pins decide how the chip starts. Something connected to them can stop uploads.
do: Unplug everything from the board except USB, and try again.
ESP32 start-up pins: GPIO 0, 2, 5, 12 and 15. ESP8266: GPIO 0, 2 and 15. Arduino Uno: D0 and D1 are the USB serial pins.
up.4.q: Does it work with nothing else connected?

l.1.why: LED strips are a chain: a fault affects everything after it.
do: Switch on and look along the strip.

a.t: Everything after one point is out or wrong
Flickers, or dim and yellowish at the far end

hot.1.why: Heat, smoke and burning smells are warnings. Stop using it before checking anything else.
do: Unplug it and don't switch it on again until you know why.

do.t: If a lithium battery is swelling, hissing or smoking, move it outside or onto a stone or metal surface away from anything that can burn. If it catches fire, call the fire service.

a.t: It smelt of burning, smoked or banged
It's just hotter than it used to be
It's just hotter than it used to be

hot.2.why: Burnt parts leave dark marks, split cases and a smell that tells you where to look.
do: Open it and look for discoloured board, split or charred parts, and melted plastic. Follow your nose.

do.t: In mains power supplies, small box-shaped 'X' or 'Y' capacitors near the mains input often crack and smoke as they age.

a.t: A cracked or burnt box capacitor near the mains input
A burnt part on the board

w.1.t: Switch it off and disconnect the power
w.1.why: Water itself does little harm. Electricity flowing through it is what causes corrosion and shorts.
do: Switch it off and unplug it. Don't try to see if it still works.

do.t: Take out the batteries.

do: Skip the bag of rice: it doesn't dry the inside, and adds dust. Opening it up and cleaning it is what works.
Sugary, salty or milky drinks corrode much faster than water, so act within hours.

w.2.why: Liquid trapped inside keeps corroding it: it needs opening up to dry and clean.

do.t: Open it and unplug the battery connector before anything else.

do: Open it up, and take out any boards you can reach easily, so both sides can dry.

w.3.why: Isopropyl alcohol shifts the residue and dries quickly.
do: Scrub every wet area with 99% isopropyl alcohol and a soft brush (a toothbrush is fine), especially connectors and the pins of chips.
An ultrasonic cleaner does a better job.

do.t: Take speakers, microphones and buzzers out before an ultrasonic clean.

do: Let it dry for at least a day somewhere warm.
Look under a magnifier for parts or tracks that have been eaten away.

a.t: Parts or tracks are eaten away

w.4.t: Put it back together and test
w.4.why: Test carefully: a short that's left can do more damage.
do: If you can, power it from a bench power supply with a low current limit first.
Test everything it does, one thing at a time.

int.1.why: If you can make the fault happen when you want, you can find it.

do.t: With it on, wiggle the cable at each end.
With it on, press gently on the battery cover and move the batteries in their springs.

do: Tap gently round the case and board with a plastic tool.
Warm it with a hair dryer, then cool it with freeze spray.

a.t: Moving it, or pressing on the battery cover

int.2.why: Leads break inside next to the plugs, where they bend the most.
do: Unplugged, set the meter to continuity and bend the lead along its length while it beeps: if the beep cuts out, that's the break.
Check the socket on the device: wobbly sockets have cracked solder joints underneath.

int.3.why: Heat and knocks crack the joints on big, heavy or hot parts.
do: Look with a magnifier at joints of sockets, transformers, regulators, heatsinks and big capacitors.
A crack is a thin dark ring round the pin, or a dull, grainy joint.

int.4.t: Warm and freeze one part at a time
int.4.why: Faulty parts often fail only when hot or cold.
do: With it running, spray freeze spray onto one part at a time, or warm one area with a hair dryer.
When the fault comes and goes as you treat a single part, you've found it.

int.5.why: Faults that come and go need a record to show the pattern.
do: Write down each time it happens: how long it had been on, how warm, and what it was doing. Use the notes box below.
Meterie can log the supply voltage over hours and show any dips.

do.t: Probie can record what the board prints over its serial connection while it runs: errors often show there.

a.t: The supply dips when it fails

tr.1.why: Overcurrent and earth leakage have different causes.
do: Look at your fuse box. An RCD (the switch with a 'T' test button) means current is leaking to earth. A breaker (MCB) or a blown plug fuse means too much current: a short.

a.t: A breaker or fuse, the moment it's switched on
Only after it's been on a while, or when damp

tr.2.t: Test for a short across the mains input
tr.2.why: A short inside the power supply makes the fuse blow straight away.
do: Unplugged, with its power switch on, measure resistance between the live and neutral pins of the plug.

do.t: Motors read a few ohms to a few hundred ohms: that's normal.

do: Electronics with a power supply should read high: thousands of ohms, often climbing as its capacitors fill.
Inside, look for a split or burnt disc (a varistor or 'MOV') and burnt X-capacitors near the mains input.
Test the bridge rectifier (four diodes, or a square block with ~ + − marks) and the switching transistor on the meter's diode test.

a.t: A split varistor or burnt X-capacitor

tr.3.why: Leakage to the earth wire usually comes from a failing part, a damaged lead or water inside.
do: Unplugged, with its switch on, measure from live and neutral (one at a time) to the earth pin.
A multimeter should read open (OL) or many megohms. An insulation tester at 500V is the proper test.

bands.say: Too low: that's a leak to earth.

r.supply.t: The power source was the problem
r.supply.cause: Whatever powers it was at fault, not the device itself.
fix: Keep using the power that works.

fix.t: If a wall socket was at fault, have it checked by an electrician.
Replace the faulty charger, adapter or lead with one that matches: same voltage, same plug, the same or more current, and from a reputable maker.
Use fresh batteries of the right type.
Replace the faulty pack or charger with one made for the tool.

r.contacts.cause: Batteries had run down, or leaked and left a crust on the contacts.
fix: Wear gloves and remove any leaking batteries.
Dab the crust with vinegar or lemon juice (it neutralises the leak from ordinary alkaline batteries), then clean with isopropyl alcohol.
Rub contacts bright with a fibreglass pen or fine sandpaper, and bend weak springs out a little.
If the crust has crept up the wires, resolder or replace them.

r.adapter.t: The adapter or charger has failed
r.adapter.cause: It isn't giving out the voltage on its label.
fix: Replace it with one of the same voltage, the same plug size and polarity (the + and − symbol on the label), and at least the same current (A).
Don't open sealed adapters: they hold mains voltage.

r.lint.t: Lint or dirt in the port
r.lint.cause: Packed fluff or dirt stopped the plug going all the way in.
fix: Keep the port clean with a wooden toothpick now and then.

fix.t: A dust plug helps if you carry it in a pocket or bag.

r.port.t: A worn or damaged charging port
r.port.cause: The contacts have worn or bent, or the port has come loose from the board.

fix.t: On many phones and tablets the port is on a separate small board or flex cable that unplugs: order the part for your exact model.

fix: If it's soldered to the main board, it needs hot air, flux and care to replace (or a repair shop).
A wobbly socket often just needs its joints resoldering.

r.flat.cause: The battery had run down below its safe level and needed time to recover.
fix: Check the battery's health (see the charging guide): if it's below about 80%, a new battery is worth it.
Avoid leaving it flat for weeks: lithium batteries are damaged by it.

r.cable.cause: The wire has broken inside, usually where it bends next to a plug.
fix: Replace the lead if it unplugs.
For a fixed lead, cut it off a little past the break and refit it, with the cord grip clamping the outer sheath. Or fit a new lead of the same rating.

fix.t: On mains leads, brown goes to live (L), blue to neutral (N), green-and-yellow to earth (E).

r.fuseok.cause: A single surge or a moment's overload.
fix: Keep an eye on it. If the new fuse blows too, something is shorted inside.
Always use the same rating.

r.burnt.cause: A part has overheated and failed, often because something after it shorted.
fix: Note its markings (resistor colour bands, a code printed on it) before removing it. A photo of a working board, or the service manual, helps if it's unreadable.
Before fitting a new one, look for why it burnt: test what it feeds for a short.
Scrape out any blackened board around it: charred board conducts.
parts: The burnt part, by its markings

r.caps.cause: Electrolytic capacitors dry out with age and heat, and then bulge or leak.
fix: Replace each one with the same capacitance (µF), the same or higher voltage, and 105°C rating.
In power supplies, use 'low-ESR' types.
Fit them the right way round: the stripe on the side is the negative leg.
Clean up any leaked electrolyte with isopropyl alcohol: it corrodes.

r.connector.cause: A cable had worked loose or wasn't fully seated.
fix: Reseat it fully, with its latch closed.
If the contacts look dull or green, clean them with isopropyl alcohol first.

r.psufuse.t: A short in the power supply
r.psufuse.cause: The fuse inside blew because a part in the power supply shorted: commonly the bridge rectifier, the switching transistor (MOSFET) or the controller chip.
fix: Don't just fit a new fuse: it will blow again, and can take more parts with it.
On the meter's diode test, check the rectifier diodes and the transistor for a short (close to 0V both ways).
Replace the shorted parts, then power it through a 'dim bulb tester' (a lamp in series) so a remaining fault can't do more damage.
Often it's easier and safer to replace the whole power supply board, by the part number on its sticker.
parts: Power supply board, or the shorted parts
r.psufuse.pro: Mains power supplies are dangerous to work on. If you're not experienced, swap the whole board or take it to a repair shop.

r.psu.cause: The power supply isn't giving out anything.

fix.t: Replace the power supply unit; any good one with enough watts and the right plugs will do.
The power supply board can usually be bought by the part number on its sticker.
Power reaches the device but its own power circuit makes nothing: check the input socket, any fuse just inside it, and the first regulator.
Check the battery's connector and the wires from it, then the power switch and the first regulator after it.

fix: If you're not confident working on power circuits, a repair shop can test it.

r.short.cause: One part has failed short and was pulling the whole rail down.
fix: Remove the warm part. Tiny ceramic capacitors fail like this often, and many boards still work without one of them for testing, but always fit a new one of the same value.
Measure the rail again: the short should be gone.

r.shortpro.cause: The short is probably under a large chip, or inside the board.
fix: Feed a little more current (carefully, 1–2A at the rail's voltage) to warm the faulty part enough to find.
Otherwise this is a job for a board-level repair shop.
r.shortpro.pro: Board-level repair needs a microscope, hot air and experience.

r.regulator.cause: The rail isn't shorted, so whatever makes it isn't doing its job.
fix: Measure the regulator's input: if the input is there and the output isn't, the regulator has failed (or its enable pin isn't being switched on).
Replace the regulator with the same part (its code is printed on it).

r.button.cause: The switch contacts have worn or got dirty.
fix: Spray contact cleaner into it and work it many times.
Replace it with the same type: small tactile switches are cheap and sold by size (6×6mm, 12×12mm…).

fix.t: Mains switches must be replaced with one rated for the same voltage and current.

r.codes.cause: The device is running and telling you what's wrong.
fix: Count the beeps or flashes and look up the pattern in the manual or the maker's support site.

fix.t: Memory and graphics faults are the commonest: reseat or swap the part.

r.board.t: A fault on the main board
r.board.cause: The simple checks are clear, so the fault is in the board's own circuits.
fix: Search for the board's part number with the fault: others have often found the cause.
With Scopie, check the crystal or clock is running. With Probie, watch the debug output many boards print at start-up.
A donor board from a broken device of the same model is often the cheapest fix.
Or take it to a board-level repair shop.

r.cooling.cause: Dust or dried thermal paste stops the heat getting out.
fix: Blow dust out with compressed air, holding the fan still so it doesn't over-spin.

fix.t: Clean off old thermal paste with isopropyl alcohol and apply a pea-sized blob of new paste.
Replace thermal pads with pads of the same thickness.
Replace a fan that's slow or noisy with one of the same size and voltage.

r.weaksupply.cause: Its power source can't keep up when the device works hard.

fix.t: Use an adapter or power supply with at least the rated watts.
Replace worn batteries.

fix: Check for thin or long cables that drop the voltage.

r.swollen.cause: Gas has built up inside: it's failing and a fire risk.
fix: Stop charging and using it now.
Remove it carefully: never puncture, bend or crush it. Soften the adhesive with isopropyl alcohol and use plastic tools only.
Store it in a metal box or on a stone floor, away from anything that burns, until you can recycle it.
Take it to a battery recycling point (most supermarkets and tips): never in household waste.
Fit a new battery from a reputable source.
r.swollen.pro: If it's very swollen or the case is cracked, many repair shops will remove it safely.

r.battery.cause: The battery has lost much of what it can hold.

fix.t: Fit a new battery from a reputable maker.
Fit a new pack from the tool's maker or a reputable brand. Rebuilding packs needs a spot welder and care.
Then charge it fully, and use it until it switches off once, so the device learns its new capacity.

r.gauge.t: It is charging: the battery reading is wrong
r.gauge.cause: The battery is healthy and takes charge, so the charge figure or light is what's wrong.

fix.t: Charge it fully, use it until it switches off, then charge it fully again without stopping: this resets the battery reading.
Charge it fully, then use it until it switches off, once or twice: many gadgets relearn their battery this way.

fix: If the light or reading still looks wrong, the battery's gauge chip or the charge light may have failed: a new battery is often the easiest fix.

r.chargeic.cause: Power reaches the device but doesn't go into the battery.
fix: Check the battery's temperature-sensor wire first.
Next is the charging chip near the port: a board-level repair.

fix.t: On laptops the charging circuit is sometimes on the separate DC-in board.

r.chargeic.pro: Charging chips are tiny and under shields: a board-level repair shop can do this.

r.backlight.cause: Backlight LEDs fail on their own, and one failed LED can put out a whole row; some boards have a backlight fuse.

fix.t: Replace the whole set of strips with a kit for your model: the others will follow the first.
Replace the fuse with the same value (bridge it only to test, then fit a proper one).
Replace the screen module: small screens have the backlight built in.

r.backlightdriver.cause: The circuit that powers the backlight isn't working.

fix.t: The driver is often on the power board: replace the board by its part number.
Check the backlight supply on the board (often marked LED+ or BL); a missing supply is a board-level repair.

fix: Replace the screen with one for your exact model.

fix.t: For phones, buy a complete assembly with the frame if you can.
TV panels usually cost too much to replace: compare with buying a new set.

r.digitizer.cause: The touch sensor itself has failed, or its cable.
fix: Reseat the touch sensor's ribbon cable first.

fix.t: On most touchscreens the touch layer is part of the screen: replace the screen assembly for your exact model.
Replace the touch pad or sensor for your exact model.

r.bond.t: The screen's ribbon or bonding has failed
r.bond.cause: Lines that change when pressed come from where the ribbon cable is bonded to the glass.
fix: This can't be fixed reliably at home. Replace the screen.

r.tcon.cause: The T-con board turns the picture signal into what the panel needs.
fix: T-con boards are cheap and swap with two ribbon cables: buy one by the part number printed on it.
Check its fuse first (often a small surface-mount fuse near the power input).

r.monitor.cause: The computer works on another monitor, so its own screen is fine.
fix: Start a new repair for the monitor itself (the closest kind is 'TV, monitor or display').
Check its cable and input setting first.

r.stepper.cause: The motor is fine, but the driver chip that powers it has failed or overheats.
fix: On boards with plug-in drivers, swap it for a spare of the same type.
On boards with soldered drivers, the mainboard usually needs replacing.
Check the driver's cooling, and its current setting (Vref) if it's adjustable.

r.ram.t: Memory or a card wasn't seated
r.ram.cause: A loose memory stick or card stops a computer starting.
fix: Reseat it firmly until the clips close. If one stick causes the fault, replace it.
Keep a note of the setting that fixed it.

r.speaker.cause: The speaker's coil has broken or shorted.
fix: Replace the speaker with one of the same impedance (Ω), size and power, or more power.

r.pot.t: A dirty volume knob or switch
r.pot.cause: Dust and oxidation inside the control make it crackle.
fix: Spray contact cleaner into the gap in the control's body, then turn it end to end 20 times.
If it's worn through, replace it with the same value (printed on it, like 'B10K').

r.hum.cause: Usually old smoothing capacitors in the power supply, or a ground loop between connected equipment.
fix: Unplug other equipment and try again: if the hum stops, it's a ground loop (a ground-loop isolator fixes it).
If it hums on its own, replace the big smoothing capacitors in the power supply.

r.distort.cause: A damaged speaker cone, or the amplifier running out of power.
fix: Check the speaker cone for tears and a scraping coil.
Check the amplifier's supply voltage holds steady when loud.

r.preamp.t: The fault is before the amplifier
r.preamp.cause: The amplifier works, so the signal is lost earlier: input socket, volume control, source switch or preamp.
fix: Follow the signal back from the amplifier to the input to find where it disappears (Scopie helps).

r.amp.cause: The amplifier chip or output transistors have failed.
fix: Check its supply voltage first.
Replace the amplifier chip (its code is printed on it), or the output transistors in pairs.
Done. Keep drinks away next time.

r.trace.cause: A copper track has cracked or corroded through.
fix: Scrape back the coating either side of the break with a knife until the copper shines.
Solder a fine wire (30 AWG) across the break, or follow the track to the next solder point.
Cover it with UV solder mask or nail varnish.

r.bearing.cause: Hair and dirt wrap round the shaft, and bearings dry out.
fix: Unplug it. Clear any hair or fluff from the shaft.
Clean the bearing and add a drop of light machine oil (not WD-40, it dries out).
If it still grinds, replace the bearing or the motor.

r.brushes.cause: The brushes press on the motor's spinning part and wear down over time.
fix: Replace both brushes with the right size for your motor (measure them, or search the model number).
Run it gently for a minute so they bed in.

r.motor.cause: A winding has broken, or the motor is worn out.
fix: Replace the motor (or fan) with the same type, voltage and size.

r.runcap.cause: Fans need a capacitor to start turning: without it they only hum.
fix: Replace it with a motor run capacitor of the same µF value and at least the same voltage (marked on it, often 450V AC).

r.thermalfuse.cause: It blew because something got too hot.
fix: Find out why first: a blocked vent, a seized motor or a stuck thermostat.
Replace it with the same temperature and current rating. Crimp it, or solder quickly with a heatsink clip: heat from the iron can blow a new one.

r.relay.cause: The part that switches the heater (a MOSFET on the board, or a relay) has failed shorted, so the heater gets full power all the time.
fix: Switch it off at the wall now, and don't use it until it's fixed: a heater stuck on is a fire risk.
Replace the heater's MOSFET or the control board. Many 3D printer owners add an external MOSFET board.
Make sure the firmware's thermal runaway protection is turned on.
r.relay.pro: If you're not sure, a heater stuck on is worth taking to someone who is.

r.element.cause: The element's wire has burnt through.
fix: Replace the heater with one of the same voltage and power (it's printed on it or in the machine's manual).

r.elementearth.cause: Something is leaking current to the metal frame or earth: dangerous.
fix: Don't use it.
Replace the faulty part, or the damaged lead.
Have it safety-tested (a PAT test) before using it again.
r.elementearth.pro: Earth faults are a shock risk: a qualified electrician or appliance repairer should test it.

r.heatdriver.t: The board isn't powering the heater
r.heatdriver.cause: The heater's fuse on the board has blown, or its switching MOSFET has failed.
fix: If the fuse blew, look for why first: a pinched heater wire touching the frame, or a shorted heater.
Replace the fuse with the same rating.
A failed MOSFET can be replaced on the board, or an external MOSFET board added; otherwise replace the mainboard.

r.thermistor.cause: The sensor wire is broken or shorted, or the sensor has failed.
fix: Check the wire along its length and the plug on the board.
Replace the thermistor with the same type (the printer's firmware expects a particular one, often a 100k NTC 3950).

r.datacable.t: A charge-only cable or a bad port
r.datacable.cause: The cable has no data wires, or the port was faulty.
fix: Label your charge-only cables so they don't get mixed up.

r.usbdata.cause: It has power, but the two data lines (D+ and D−) aren't getting through cleanly.
fix: Try another cable and port first.
Inside, check the USB socket's joints and the small protection chip next to it.

r.driver.cause: The computer can see it but doesn't know what to do with it.
fix: Install the driver or app from the device's maker.

fix.t: For boards with a USB-serial chip: WCH for CH340, Silicon Labs for CP210x, FTDI for FT232.

fix: Restart the computer, then try again.

r.bootmode.cause: The board wasn't switching into upload mode on its own.
fix: Use the button sequence each time, or fit a 10µF capacitor between EN and GND on ESP32 boards that never switch on their own.

r.strap.cause: Something connected to a start-up pin stopped the chip entering upload mode.
fix: Move that wiring to a different pin, or disconnect it while uploading.

r.mcu.cause: The chip or its regulator has failed.
fix: Check its 3.3V or 5V supply for a short.
Development boards are cheap: replacing it is usually best.

r.ledjoint.t: A bad joint or LED in the strip
r.ledjoint.cause: The connection, or the first LED where the fault starts, has failed.
fix: Press on the joint: if it flickers back, resolder it.
Otherwise cut out that segment at the copper pads and solder in a new piece.

r.voltdrop.cause: Long strips lose voltage along their thin copper.
fix: Feed power in at both ends, and every 2–5 metres along long runs.
Use thicker wire to the strip, and a supply with enough current.

r.ledchannel.cause: The controller's driver for that colour, or a wire, has failed.
fix: Check the wire for that colour from the controller. Swap two colour wires to see whether the fault moves.
Replace the controller if the fault stays with its output.

r.x2.cause: The X or Y capacitor across the mains has aged and burnt.
fix: Replace it only with an X2-rated (or Y-rated, if that's what it was) capacitor of the same value. Never an ordinary capacitor.

r.melt.cause: A poor contact got hot and melted the plastic.
fix: Replace both halves of the connector, and the wire up to clean copper.
Use a connector rated for the current.

r.mov.cause: The varistor (MOV) or X-capacitor shorted after a surge.
fix: Replace it with the same type and voltage, and check the fuse.
If there was a big surge, check other parts too.
Keep an eye on it for a few weeks: corrosion can carry on in places you couldn't reach.

r.corrosion.cause: The liquid ate away parts or connections.
fix: Replace damaged connectors and flex cables.
Repair eaten tracks with fine wire.
Replace small parts that have gone (you'll need the board diagram).

r.joint.cause: Heat and movement have cracked the solder.
fix: Add a little flux and reflow each joint with a hot iron (about 350°C for leaded solder, 380°C for lead-free) and a bit of fresh solder.
For old lead-free joints, adding some leaded solder helps it flow.

r.thermalpart.t: A part that fails with temperature
r.thermalpart.cause: You found the part that misbehaves when hot or cold.
fix: Replace it. Reflow its joints first if it's large: often it's the joint, not the part.

r.pro.cause: This fault needs mains-safety training or special equipment.
fix: Have it tested by an appliance repairer or electrician (a PAT test checks earth and insulation).
Note down everything you've checked so far: it saves them time.

b.vis.1.why: Many faults are visible: a few minutes with a light and magnifier saves hours of measuring.

do.t: Unplug it, wait a few minutes, and check the big capacitors are discharged before touching anything.
Disconnect the battery first.

do: Photograph both sides of the board: useful later, and for asking for help.
Look under a bright light, at an angle, with a magnifier: burnt or cracked parts, bulging capacitors, corrosion, cracked joints, damaged tracks, missing parts.
Note the part numbers of the main chips: their datasheets show the pins to measure.

b.in.1.why: Start at the input: everything else depends on it.

do.t: For a mains board, measure the low-voltage outputs of its power supply instead (never the mains side). If they're missing, go to the Mains power supply section.
Power it as normal. Measure the voltage on the input connector, black probe on its ground.

a.t: No, it's missing at the connector
No: a mains board's supply gives nothing

apps.how: DC volts. Watch the graph while you wiggle the plug: a dip shows a loose socket.
