b.in.2.why: Just inside the input there's usually a fuse, a diode against reversed power, and a clamp. Any can stop or short the power.
do: Measure on the far side of each part in turn: the fuse (or polyfuse), then the diode.
A diode drops about 0.3–0.7V; a fuse should drop almost nothing.

a.t: After the fuse: it's blown or tripped
It gets through, but the voltage is pulled low

apps.how: DC volts; move the red probe along the path, keeping the black on ground.

b.in.3.why: A fuse blows because something after it drew too much: find that before fitting a new one.
do: Power off. Measure resistance from the far side of the fuse to ground.
Under about 10Ω: something is shorted. Check the protection diode or TVS and the input capacitors first: they're the commonest culprits.

a.t: A shorted protection diode or TVS
Shorted, but I can't find where

r.diodeopen.cause: The diode against reversed power has failed open.
fix: Replace it with the same type, or one with the same or higher current and the same or lower voltage drop (a Schottky in, Schottky out).

r.tvs.cause: A TVS diode or protection diode shorted to protect the rest from a spike or reversed power.
fix: Remove it: if the short goes, that was it.
Fit a new one of the same type and voltage before using it for real: it's what protects the rest.
Fit a new fuse of the same rating.

r.fuseonly.cause: Nothing is shorted now: probably a one-off surge, or a fault that cleared.
fix: Fit the same rating of fuse.

fix.t: Power it from a current-limited supply the first time.
Power it through a dim bulb tester the first time.

fix: If it blows again, the fault comes on under power: measure the rails as it starts.

b.smps.1.t: Cold tests on the power supply
b.smps.1.why: Most mains power supply faults show up with the power off: start here, it's safer.
do: Unplugged. Wait, then measure across the big capacitor: below about 5V before you touch anything. Discharge it with a resistor if not.
Fuse: continuity. Bridge rectifier: four diode tests. The big switching MOSFET: drain-source not shorted.
Look for the startup resistors (high values like 470k–2M feeding the controller chip): they drift open with age, a common cause of a supply that's completely dead.

a.t: A blown fuse and a shorted MOSFET or rectifier
A startup resistor open or high

b.smps.2.why: Faults on the low-voltage side make a supply shut itself down: it ticks, chirps or cycles.
do: Power off. Diode-test the output rectifier diodes (often a dual Schottky on a heatsink): a short is common.
ESR-test the output capacitors: dried ones cause cycling and noise.
Check each output for a short to ground.

a.t: A shorted output (the fault is in what it feeds)

b.smps.3.why: With the cold tests passed, power the supply through a dim bulb tester so a remaining fault can't do damage.
do: Connect it through a dim bulb tester. Keep hands off the board; use clip leads on the low-voltage outputs only.
Watch the bulb: a flash then dim is normal; bright and staying bright means a short is still there.
Measure the outputs (low-voltage side only), and listen for ticking.

a.t: It ticks or the outputs pulse

apps.how: DC volts on the low-voltage output, with the graph running: pulsing outputs show as a saw-tooth.

r.startres.cause: The controller chip never gets enough voltage to start, usually because its high-value startup resistors have drifted open, or its supply capacitor has dried out.
fix: Measure the startup resistors out of the circuit and replace any that read high or open.
Replace the small electrolytic on the controller's supply pin (VCC/VDD): a very common fault.
If it still won't start, replace the controller chip.
r.startres.pro: This is on the mains side of the board: work only with it unplugged and the big capacitor discharged.

r.schottky.cause: The rectifier on the low-voltage side has failed short, so the supply shuts down.
fix: Replace it with the same part (or the same voltage and current, Schottky for Schottky).
Check the output capacitors too: they often failed first.

r.feedback.t: The supply's feedback or output stage
r.feedback.cause: It starts, but cycles: the voltage feedback (optocoupler and TL431) or a dried output capacitor makes it shut down and restart.
fix: Replace the output capacitors if not done.
Test the optocoupler and the TL431 reference (often a 3-leg part near the opto).
Check nothing on the outputs draws too much: disconnect the load and try again.

b.reg.1.why: Each chip runs from a rail. A missing or low rail points straight at the fault.
do: Find the rails: labels like 5V, 3V3, 1V8, VCC, test points, or the regulators' outputs (look up their pinouts).
Measure each with the device on, black probe on a solid ground.

apps.how: DC volts. Use the min/max hold to catch a rail that dips at start-up.

b.reg.2.t: Find why a rail is missing
b.reg.2.why: Missing means the regulator isn't making it, or it's switched off.
do: Measure the regulator's input: if that's missing, go back a step along the power path.
Switching regulators: is the enable pin high? Some rails are switched on by the processor: they stay off if it isn't running.
Power off and measure the rail to ground: a short makes the regulator shut down.

a.t: The rail is shorted to ground
Input and enable fine, no output

b.reg.3.why: A shorted part pulls a rail down and gets warm when power is pushed into it.
do: Power off. Measure the rail to ground: compare with a similar rail; a few ohms or less is a short.
Feed the rail from a bench power supply at its voltage, current limit at 0.5–1A.
Find the warm part: thermal camera, a film of isopropyl alcohol that dries first, or freeze spray that melts first. Small ceramic capacitors are the usual cause.

b.bat.1.t: Measure the battery and its protection
b.bat.1.why: Battery packs have a protection board that cuts the output when a cell goes too low or too high.
do: Measure the pack at its output, then each cell (or cell group) directly.
Single cells: 3.0–4.2V is normal. A pack that reads 0V at its output with healthy cells has its protection tripped.

a.t: A cell or group much lower than the rest

apps.how: DC volts on each cell in turn; note them in the step's notes.

b.bat.2.why: If the cells are fine, the charge chip or its sensing is next.
do: With the charger connected, measure the charger's input on the board, then the battery voltage: it should slowly rise.
Look up the charge chip: check its status pin (it often drives the charge LED) and its temperature-sense pin (a missing thermistor stops charging).

r.bmstrip.cause: The protection board cut the output after the pack went too low, or saw a short.
fix: Connect the proper charger: many wake up a tripped pack.
If not, the board may need a brief connection to a charger at the pack's own voltage; only if you know Li-ion safety.
If cells are below 2.5V, see Parts tests: lithium-ion cell.
r.bmstrip.salvage: If the pack is done for, healthy cells can be reused in projects with a new protection board: test each one (Parts tests).

r.cellbad.cause: One cell or group has lost capacity or self-discharges, and drags the whole pack down.
fix: Replace the pack, or rebuild it with matched new cells (a spot welder is needed: never solder directly to cells).
r.cellbad.salvage: The other cells may be good: test each one before reusing it.

b.clk.1.why: A processor does nothing without its clock.
do: Find the crystal or oscillator next to the main chip (a metal can or a small box marked with a frequency).
Use a ×10 probe on the output side (XOUT, XTAL2, OSC_OUT): ×1 probes can stop it.

a.t: A clean wave at the marked frequency
A wave, but the wrong frequency

apps.how: ×10 probe, timebase so a few cycles fill the screen, trigger on CH1, turn on Frequency.

b.clk.2.why: If the reset or enable line is held, the chip waits forever. If it pulses, the chip keeps restarting.
do: Find the reset pin (RESET, RST, NRST, often with a small capacitor and pull-up, or a 3-pin supervisor chip).
Measure it with the device on: most chips run when it's high.
Watch it over a few seconds with a scope or logic analyser: repeated pulses mean something keeps resetting it (a watchdog, or a supply dipping).

apps.how: Logic tab: one channel on the reset pin, capture several seconds at a low sample rate (10kHz) to see any pulses.
Slow timebase (500ms/div), roll mode, CH1 on reset.

r.crystal.cause: The crystal, its two small capacitors, or the chip's oscillator has failed.
fix: Reflow the crystal's joints (they crack in dropped devices).
Replace the crystal with the same frequency and type, and check the two load capacitors.
If it still doesn't run, the processor's oscillator may have failed.

r.reset.cause: The reset supervisor or its pull-up holds the chip in reset, usually because it sees a low supply, or the supervisor has failed.
fix: Check the supply the supervisor watches is at its full voltage.
Check the pull-up resistor and the reset capacitor (a shorted capacitor holds reset low).
Replace the supervisor chip if its input is fine but its output is low.

b.cpu.1.why: With power, clock and reset right, look for signs of life.
do: Find a serial TX pin or debug header (often 3–4 pins marked TX, RX, GND, or unlabeled pads near the chip).
Connect a USB-serial adapter (the board's TX to its RX, grounds together) at the board's voltage, and power up.
Or capture several of the chip's pins with a logic analyser: any switching shows it's running.

a.t: Boot messages that stop with an error

apps.how: Serial tab: pick the adapter's port, try 115200 then 9600; Explain describes errors in plain words. Logic tab: 4–8 channels on the chip's pins, 1MHz sample rate.

b.cpu.2.why: A boot loop is usually power dipping when something switches on, or a watchdog firing.
do: Watch the main rail with a scope (or Meterie's min/max) during start-up: a dip at the moment it restarts points at the supply.
Read the boot messages: many chips print the reset reason (brownout, watchdog).

apps.how: CH1 on the main rail, single trigger on a falling edge set just below the rail voltage.
Serial tab: the reset reason is usually near the start of the boot messages.

r.bootlog.t: The boot messages show the fault
r.bootlog.cause: The processor runs, and is telling you where it stops.
fix: Note the last lines before it stops: a missing part on a bus, a memory test failure, a storage error.
Search for that message with the device's model: others often know it.
Use Probie's Explain to turn the error into plain words.

r.firmware.cause: Power, clock and reset are fine, but the program in flash memory is damaged, or the chip has failed.
fix: Back up whatever is on the flash chip first with a programmer.
Reflash with the maker's firmware or a backup from an identical device.
If it still doesn't run, the processor (or the flash chip) has failed.
r.firmware.salvage: If it can't be revived, the rest of the board often isn't: but displays, motors, connectors and power parts usually are.

r.weakrail.cause: The rail sags when something starts, and the processor resets: dried capacitors or a weak regulator.
fix: Replace electrolytic capacitors on that rail and at the regulator.
Check the regulator's input holds up too.
Add bulk capacitance near whatever draws the surge, if it's a design weakness.

b.bus.1.why: Chips talk over a few shared wires. Decoding the traffic shows which part isn't answering.
do: Identify the bus: I2C has SDA and SCL (two wires with pull-up resistors); SPI has CLK, MOSI, MISO and a chip-select per device; UART has TX and RX.
Clip the logic analyser's ground to the board's ground and one channel to each wire.
Capture during start-up, when the processor talks to everything.

a.t: I2C: an address gets NAK (no answer)
I2C: lines stay low, or no clean edges
SPI: data out, but nothing comes back

apps.how: Logic tab: add the I2C, SPI or UART decoder; sample rate at least 4× the bus speed (2MHz for 400kHz I2C). Explain summarises who answered.

b.bus.2.why: A NAK means nobody answered at that address: the chip has no power, isn't connected, or has failed.
do: Find the chip with that address (its datasheet lists it).
Check its power pins and ground.
Check continuity from SDA and SCL on the processor to the same pins on the chip.

a.t: A break in SDA or SCL

b.bus.3.why: I2C lines are pulled high by resistors and pulled low by the chips. A shorted chip or missing pull-up stops the whole bus.
do: With the device on and idle, both SDA and SCL should read close to the supply voltage.
If one is stuck low, power off and disconnect or lift chips one at a time until it frees: the last one removed is the culprit.
Slow, rounded rising edges on a scope mean the pull-ups are too weak (or missing).

a.t: A chip holds the line low
Lines idle high, edges are clean

apps.how: CH1 on SDA, CH2 on SCL, about 2µs/div: edges should rise quickly and square.

r.chippower.cause: Its supply pin is dead, so it can't answer.
fix: Follow its supply pin back to the rail it comes from: a broken track, a missing ferrite bead or resistor in series, or a rail that's switched off.
If the whole rail is missing, go to the Regulators and rails section.

r.nocontrol.t: Nothing is telling it to switch
r.nocontrol.cause: The control signal never changes, so the fault is before the driver.
fix: Check continuity from the processor's pin to the driver's input (resistors in between too).
If the processor isn't running at all, go to the Processor and memory section.

r.noinput.cause: Power stops somewhere between the input and this regulator.
fix: Follow its input pin back towards the power input, measuring at each part: a fuse, a diode, a switch, a ferrite or a broken track.
The Power input and protection section goes through the usual parts.

r.busdev.t: A chip on the bus has failed
r.busdev.cause: It doesn't answer, or holds the bus.
fix: Reflow its joints first.
Replace it with the same part (and the same address variant).

r.pullup.cause: Without its pull-up, the line can't return high.
fix: Replace the resistor (usually 2.2k–10k to the supply).

r.spidev.cause: Its chip-select, power, or the chip itself.
fix: Check its chip-select line goes low when it's addressed, and its power.
Check MISO continuity back to the processor.
Replace the chip (memory chips: back up and reprogram).

r.baud.t: Serial speed or level is wrong
r.baud.cause: Garbled characters mean the speed doesn't match, or the voltage levels don't (RS-232 vs logic level).
fix: Measure one bit's width in the capture: 1 ÷ width = the baud rate.
RS-232 swings to ±5–12V; logic-level serial is 0–3.3V or 0–5V: a level converter (MAX232 type) may have failed.

b.aud.1.why: Following a known signal through the circuit shows exactly where it stops.
do: Play a 1kHz tone into the input (a tone-generator app on a phone works), at a low volume.
Put the scope's ground on the board's audio ground.
Start at the input socket, then follow the signal: each coupling capacitor, each op-amp or transistor stage, the volume control, the amplifier chip, then the speaker.

a.t: At a capacitor (there on one side, not the other)
At an op-amp or transistor stage

bands.say: Practically nothing: the signal stops before here.

apps.how: CH1, about 500µs/div, AC coupling, Peak-to-peak on. Move the probe along the path.

b.aud.2.t: Check the stage's power and bias
b.aud.2.why: Every amplifying stage needs its supply, and sits at a resting voltage with no signal.
do: Measure the op-amp's supply pins, or the transistor's collector and emitter.
With no signal, op-amp outputs rest mid-way (0V on a ± supply, half the supply on a single one).

a.t: Output stuck at a supply rail

b.aud.3.why: Amplifier chips need power, and many have a mute or standby pin the processor controls.
do: Supply pins at the right voltage.
Find the MUTE, STBY or SD pin in the datasheet: is it in the 'play' state?
With no signal, measure DC across the speaker terminals: more than about 50mV means a faulty output stage.

r.couplecap.cause: Small electrolytics between stages dry out and stop passing the signal: very common in old audio.
fix: Replace the electrolytics in the signal path (a 'recap'), same µF and voltage or higher.
Film capacitors are a good replacement for small values.
Replace the op-amp with the same or a pin-compatible part.
Check its supply rails are both present first.

r.mute.cause: The mute or standby pin keeps it silent: usually the processor holding it, or a fault the processor detected.
fix: Follow the mute pin back to what drives it.
Check the processor is running (Processor and memory).
Briefly tying it to the 'play' level shows whether the amplifier works.

b.vid.1.why: Every video signal carries timing pulses. If they're there, the video circuit is running.
do: Composite video (yellow socket): about 1V peak to peak, with sync pulses every 64µs (15.6–15.7kHz).
VGA: separate horizontal sync (about 31.5kHz for 640×480) and vertical sync (50–75Hz), on pins 13 and 14.
Probe the output socket first, then back towards the video chip.

a.t: Sync is there at the right rate

apps.how: Composite: CH1, 20µs/div, trigger on the falling sync edge. VGA: 10µs/div on HSYNC.
VGA or digital sync: one channel each on HSYNC and VSYNC; the frequency shows in the measurement.

b.vid.2.why: With sync right, look at the picture part of the signal.
do: Composite: the picture rides above the sync, up to about 0.7V above black.
VGA: each of R, G and B swings 0 to 0.7V; a missing colour channel means that colour's output stage.
Check the 75Ω terminations and output resistors in the path.

a.t: One colour or the picture part is missing
Levels right: the fault's in the screen or cable

apps.how: CH1 on each colour pin in turn at 10µs/div; turn on Peak-to-peak.

b.vid.3.t: Check the video chip's supply and clock
b.vid.3.why: No sync means the video chip isn't running.
do: Measure its supply pins, and look for its own clock (often a separate crystal: 14.318MHz, 17.734MHz, 25.175MHz…).
Check it's out of reset or enabled.

r.vidclock.cause: The video chip's clock is off, or it's set to a mode the display can't show.
fix: Check the video crystal's frequency.
Some devices switch PAL/NTSC with a jumper or setting: check it.

r.vidout.cause: The output transistor, buffer chip, or a resistor in the path has failed.
fix: Follow the missing signal back to the first point it's present, and test the parts between (Parts tests).
Replace the failed transistor, resistor or buffer.

b.out.1.t: Is the output being told to switch?
b.out.1.why: Every driven output has a control signal. Check that first: it tells you whether the fault is before or after the driver.
do: Find the driver (a transistor, MOSFET, driver chip, or relay) for the thing that doesn't work.
Watch its control input (transistor base, MOSFET gate, chip's IN pin) while you ask the device to switch it.

a.t: Yes, but the output doesn't follow

apps.how: One channel on the control pin; PWM outputs show their frequency and duty in the measurement.

b.out.2.why: The control works, so the driver or the load has failed.
do: Power off. Test the transistor or MOSFET (Parts tests); test the relay's coil and contacts.

do.t: Check the flyback diode across motors and relay coils: when it fails, the driver fails with it.
Check the flyback diode across any relay coil it drives: when it fails, the driver fails with it.

do: Test the load itself (whatever it switches) on its own.

r.driver2.t: A failed driver transistor or MOSFET
r.driver2.cause: It's shorted (output stuck on) or open (never switches).
fix: Replace it with the same part or an equivalent (Parts tests: transistor, MOSFET).
Replace the flyback diode too if there is one.
Find why it failed: a shorted load or a missing diode kills the new one.

r.load.cause: Whatever the driver switches (an LED, lamp, solenoid, relay coil or module) has failed.
fix: Test it on its own from a suitable supply.
Replace it with the same type and rating.

r.relay2.cause: The coil is open, or the contacts are burnt or welded.
fix: Replace it with the same coil voltage and contact rating.
r.relay2.salvage: Working relays from scrapped boards are worth keeping: test them first (Parts tests).

b.inp.1.why: Buttons are read directly or by scanning a matrix; sensors give a voltage or a digital signal.
do: Single buttons: measure the input pin while pressing: it should swing between its two levels (often pulled high, pressed = low).
Keyboard matrices: the processor pulses each row in turn and reads the columns. Capture a row and a column while holding a key.
Analog sensors and pots: measure the voltage at the processor's input as you change them.

a.t: It changes but the device ignores it

apps.how: Logic tab: one channel per row and column, 100kHz sample rate, capture while holding a key: the pressed key joins its row and column.

b.inp.2.t: Test the switch and its path
b.inp.2.why: The switch, its pull-up, or the track to the processor.
do: Power off. Continuity across the switch while pressing.
Check the pull-up resistor (often 10k).
Continuity from the switch to the processor's pin.

b.con.1.why: Breaks in cables, flex, tracks and vias stop signals and power reaching where they're needed.
do: Power off. Continuity from each pin of the connector to where it goes on each board.
Flex cables: look for creases and cracks; bend them gently while beeping.
Vias (small plated holes) corrode through after a spill: beep from one side of the board to the other.

apps.how: Continuity with the graph: a break that only opens when bent shows as a gap.

u.pw.1.t: Measure the supply at your board
u.pw.1.why: Check the voltage where it's used, not just at the supply.
do: Power it on. Measure across the supply pins of your main board or chip (VCC/5V/3V3 to GND).
On a breadboard, measure the power rails at both ends: long breadboards split their rails in the middle.

a.t: Much lower than it should be

apps.how: DC volts; the min/max hold catches a supply that drops when it starts.

u.pw.2.t: Follow the power from the source
do: Measure at the supply itself, then at each point along the way: connector, switch, fuse, regulator in and out.

do.t: Barrel plugs: check the adapter's polarity matches what your circuit expects (most are centre positive).

do: Breadboards: is the rail you're using actually connected? Wire jumper across the gap in split rails.
Regulators: check the pinout. A 7805 is IN-GND-OUT; an AMS1117 is GND-OUT-IN: fitting one like the other is a very common mistake.

a.t: At the supply: it gives nothing
At a regulator: wrong pinout or way round
At a connector, switch or wire

u.pw.3.why: Too much current means a short or a part in backwards; none at all means something's open.
do: Power it from a bench supply with the current limit set low (100–200mA to start), or put the meter in series on its current range.
Compare with what you'd expect: a bare dev board draws 20–100mA.

a.t: Hits the current limit or far too much

bands.say: Plausible for a small build: compare with what you expected.
A lot: look for a short or a reversed part.

u.pw.4.why: Low voltage at the board means the supply can't keep up, or something pulls it down.

do.t: Disconnect parts of the circuit one at a time (motors, LEDs, modules) and watch the voltage.
Disconnect parts of the circuit one at a time (LEDs, modules, displays) and watch the voltage.

do: Long, thin wires drop voltage under load: measure at both ends of each.

do.t: USB ports give 500mA (USB 2) to 900mA (USB 3): heavy loads need their own supply.

a.t: The supply can't give enough current

r.pinout.t: A part fitted the wrong way, or the wrong pinout
r.pinout.cause: Regulators, transistors and chips with the same package often have different pinouts.
fix: Check the datasheet's pinout against your wiring, with the part's flat face or notch matched to the drawing.
Test the part after a power-up the wrong way: regulators and chips often survive, but not always (Parts tests).

u.hot.1.why: A hot part is either shorted, fitted backwards, or working too hard.
do: Power off at once if anything smells or smokes.
Power it from a current-limited supply and feel for warmth with the back of a finger, or use a thermal camera.
Check orientation of everything with a polarity: electrolytic capacitors, diodes, LEDs, regulators, chips (pin 1 dot or notch).

a.t: A regulator, but it's fitted right
A transistor or MOSFET driving a load

u.hot.2.why: A linear regulator burns off the difference as heat: (input − output) × current.
do: Measure its input and output voltage, and the current through it.
Example: 12V in, 5V out at 200mA is (12 − 5) × 0.2 = 1.4W: too much for a small regulator without a heatsink (a bare TO-220 manages about 1W; SOT-223 well under 1W).

a.t: Yes, more than it can shed

u.hot.3.t: Check the driver is switching fully
u.hot.3.why: A transistor or MOSFET that's only half on gets hot.
do: Measure the gate (MOSFET) or base current (transistor) drive: a MOSFET driven from 3.3V needs a 'logic-level' type.
Measure the voltage across it while on: more than a few tenths of a volt at real current means it isn't fully on.

do.t: Motors and relays need a flyback diode across them.
Relay coils need a flyback diode across them.

r.reghot.t: The regulator is working too hard
r.reghot.cause: Too big a drop at too much current.
fix: Use a buck converter module instead: they waste very little.
Or lower the input voltage, add a heatsink, or split the load.

r.logiclevel.t: The MOSFET isn't fully switched on
r.logiclevel.cause: Standard MOSFETs need about 10V on the gate; 3.3V or 5V leaves them half on.
fix: Use a logic-level MOSFET (look for RDS(on) quoted at VGS = 2.5V or 4.5V), or drive the gate through a transistor or driver.

r.flyback.cause: Relay coils and other inductive loads kick back a high voltage spike when switched off.
fix: Fit a diode across the coil, band to the positive side: a 1N4148 for small relays, a 1N400x or a Schottky for bigger coils.

fix.t: DC motors need one too, across the motor's terminals.

r.heatsink.cause: It's switching properly but carries enough current to heat up.
fix: Add a heatsink, or use a part with a lower on-resistance.

u.code.1.t: Prove the board runs at all
u.code.1.why: Before your code, check the board can run the simplest thing.
do: Upload a blink sketch (or the board's 'hello world') and nothing else.
Add a print at the very start of your program, and open the serial monitor at the matching speed.

apps.how: Serial tab at your sketch's speed: prints show how far it gets; Explain describes crash messages.

do: Add a print before and after each part of your setup: the last message tells you where it stops.
Common stops: waiting for a sensor that isn't there (I2C begin), a library expecting different pins, a loop that never ends.

a.t: At pin setup or a library

apps.how: Serial tab: watch the prints as it starts.

u.code.3.why: A reset loop is a power dip (brownout), a crash, or a watchdog.
do: Read the first lines it prints after each restart: ESP32 and ESP8266 print the reset reason (brownout, panic, watchdog).
Watch the supply with a scope while it resets: a dip when something heavy switches on is a brownout.

apps.how: CH1 on the 3.3V or 5V pin, single trigger on a falling edge just below the rail.
Serial tab at 115200 (74880 for ESP8266 boot messages).

r.crash.cause: A crash message (panic, exception, stack trace) shows where.
fix: Decode the backtrace (the ESP exception decoder turns addresses into line numbers).
Common causes: an array written past its end, a null pointer, too little stack for a big local array, a library used before begin().

r.watchdog.cause: A loop runs too long without letting the system do its own work.
fix: Add a short delay or yield() in long loops; never wait forever for a sensor.
On ESP32, avoid long blocking work in callbacks and interrupts.

u.bus.1.why: Before the data, check the module answers at all.
do: I2C: run an I2C scanner sketch. It lists every address that answers.
Check the module's power and ground, and that SDA and SCL go to the right pins for your board (they differ between boards).

a.t: A different address from my code
The right address, but readings are wrong
It's SPI or serial, not I2C

apps.how: Logic tab: SDA and SCL on two channels with the I2C decoder; NAK after the address means nothing answered.

do: SDA and SCL swapped is the commonest mistake.
I2C needs pull-up resistors (2.2k–10k to the supply). Many modules include them; a bare chip doesn't.
Measure SDA and SCL with everything idle: both should sit near the supply voltage.
A 5V module on a 3.3V board may need a level shifter.

u.bus.3.why: It answers, so look at what it's saying.
do: Capture a reading with the logic analyser and the bus decoder: compare the bytes with the datasheet.
Check your code reads the right registers, in the right order, and converts them as the datasheet says (byte order, signed values, scale).

a.t: The data looks right: my conversion is wrong
The data is wrong or noisy

apps.how: Logic tab with the I2C or SPI decoder; Explain lists each read and write.

u.bus.4.why: SPI needs the right mode and chip-select; serial needs matching speed and crossed wires.
do: SPI: check chip-select goes low around each transfer, and the clock mode (0–3) matches the datasheet.
Serial: TX goes to RX and RX to TX; both sides at the same speed and voltage.

apps.how: Logic tab: SPI decoder (set the mode) or UART decoder; it can measure the bit width to find the baud rate.

r.i2caddr.t: The address in your code is wrong
r.i2caddr.cause: Many modules have two possible addresses, set by a pin or solder jumper.
fix: Use the address the scanner found, or change the module's address pin to match your code.

r.levels.cause: 3.3V boards can be damaged by 5V signals, and may not read 3.3V as high on 5V parts.
fix: Use a level shifter, or run the module at 3.3V if it supports it.

r.convert.t: The data is right, the conversion isn't
r.convert.cause: The module sends good data; the code reads it wrongly.
fix: Check byte order (high byte first?), signed values, and the scale factor in the datasheet.
Try the library's example sketch to compare.

u.wire.1.t: Check your build against your design
u.wire.1.why: Go through every connection, one at a time, with the power off.
do: With your schematic or Wirie design open, beep out each connection from part to part, ticking them off.
Then check neighbouring pins on each chip and header aren't shorted together.

do.t: Check pin numbering: board labels (D4, GPIO2) aren't the same as chip pin numbers.
Check pin numbering against each part's datasheet, counting from pin 1.

do: On a breadboard, check each wire is in the row you think: the five holes in a row are joined, and the centre gap separates the two sides.

a.t: A wire on the wrong pin

apps.how: Open your design; follow each net in the PCB tab and beep it out.
Continuity beep, so you can keep your eyes on the board.

r.solderbridge.cause: Solder or a stray strand joins two pins.
fix: Remove it with solder wick and flux, then check again with the meter.
Look under a magnifier at every fine-pitch joint.

u.sig.1.why: A scope or logic analyser shows exactly what the signal does, not what you hope it does.
do: Ground clip to your circuit's ground, probe on the signal.
Check it's there, its voltage levels, its frequency or timing, and its shape (clean edges, no ringing or noise).

apps.how: Autoset, then turn on Frequency, Peak-to-peak and Duty cycle.
Digital signals: the measurement shows frequency and duty cycle.

u.sig.2.why: Wrong frequency usually comes from settings, not hardware.
do: PWM: check the frequency and resolution settings in your code (servos want 50Hz, 1–2ms pulses).
Clocks: the board's clock setting in your software (8MHz vs 16MHz boards run everything at the wrong speed).
Video: sync timing must match the standard exactly.

apps.how: Measure the pulse width and frequency on the Logic tab.

r.sigmissing.cause: Nothing appears where the signal should be.
fix: Check the pin in your code is set as an output, and is the pin you've wired (board labels differ from chip numbers).
Probe right at the chip's pin: if it's there, follow the wire; if not, it's the code or pin setup.
Beep out the wiring against your design (I think something's wired wrong).

r.clipping.cause: The signal is bigger than the stage can handle, or the stage isn't biased in the middle.
fix: Lower the input level, or the gain.
Check the stage's resting voltage is about half its supply (single-supply circuits).
Check coupling capacitors are the right way round.

u.noise.1.t: Watch the supply when the load switches
u.noise.1.why: Loads that switch on hard draw surges that pull the supply down or put spikes on it.
do: Scope on your board's supply pin, trigger on a falling edge just below the supply, then switch the load on.
Check each chip has a 100nF capacitor right next to its power pins, and there's a bigger one (100–1000µF) where the load's power enters.

do.t: Motors and relays: is there a flyback diode? Do they share a thin ground wire with your logic?
Relays: is there a flyback diode across each coil? Does the load share a thin ground wire with your logic?

apps.how: CH1 on the supply, single trigger, 1ms/div to start; zoom in on the dip.

r.pickup.t: Noise picked up on the signal wires
r.pickup.cause: The supply is clean, so interference gets in on the signals themselves.
fix: Keep signal wires short and away from power wiring; twist each signal with a ground wire.
Add pull-up or pull-down resistors to inputs that float.
Filter slow signals (an RC filter) and average sensor readings in code.

r.decouple.cause: The supply sags or spikes when the load switches.
fix: Add 100nF ceramic capacitors at every chip's power pins.
Add bulk capacitance (100–1000µF) where the load's power comes in.
Give heavy loads their own supply, joined to your logic only at ground.

r.ground.t: Ground shared with a heavy load
r.ground.cause: Load current through a shared ground wire shifts your logic's ground.
fix: Run the load's ground straight back to the supply, and join logic ground at one point.
Use thicker wire for load current.

u.mot.1.t: Check the motor's supply and driver
u.mot.1.why: Motors need far more current than a board pin can give: always through a driver.
do: Measure the motor supply while it tries to move: does it sag?
Driver boards: check enable pins and that its logic supply is there.
Steppers: find the two coil pairs (each pair reads a few ohms; different pairs read OL) and wire each pair to one driver output.
Servos: they need 50Hz pulses, 1–2ms wide, and their own 5–6V supply.

apps.how: Servo signal: the measurement should show about 50Hz and 5–10% duty.

u.mot.2.why: Stepper drivers have a current limit; too low skips, too high overheats.
do: Set the driver's current limit (Vref) for your motor's rated current, from the driver's datasheet.
Check microstepping jumpers match your code.
Too fast acceleration makes steppers stall: start slower.

u.led.1.t: Check data level, resistor and power
u.led.1.why: Addressable LEDs are fussy about their data signal and their supply.
do: Data voltage: a 3.3V board driving 5V LEDs often works badly. Use a level shifter (74AHCT125), or power the first LED a little lower.
Fit a 300–500Ω resistor in the data line at the first LED, and a 1000µF capacitor across the supply.
Join the LED supply's ground to the board's ground.
Check the colour order (RGB vs GRB) and LED type in your code.

a.t: Flicker or wrong colours at the far end

apps.how: CH1 on the data line at the first LED, 1µs/div: pulses should be clean and reach near the LED supply voltage.

tools.name: Multimeter
tools.why: Measures voltage, resistance and continuity: the main tool for finding faults.
how: DC volts (V⎓): black probe on ground, red on the point to measure. Use auto-range, or a range above what you expect.
Continuity (the beep or speaker symbol): beeps when two points are connected. Only on unplugged circuits.
Resistance (Ω): unplugged only. Parts still on the board may read lower, because of what's around them.
Diode test: a good diode reads about 0.5–0.7V one way and open (OL) the other. Close to 0V both ways is a short.
tools.appWhy: Meterie shows your meter on the computer and logs it over time.

tools.name: Precision screwdriver set
tools.why: Small devices use tiny and special screws.
how: Get a set with Phillips PH000–PH1, Torx T3–T10 (including security Torx with a hole), pentalobe for iPhones, and tri-point for consoles.
Push down firmly while turning: stripped screws are the hardest thing to recover from.

tools.name: Plastic pry tools and picks
tools.why: Open clips and glued seams without scratching or shorting anything.
how: Use plastic for anything near the battery or board.
Thin guitar-pick-style picks slide into glued seams.

tools.name: Bright torch
tools.why: Inspection needs strong, angled light.
how: Shine it low and from the side to show cracks, bulges and corrosion.

tools.name: Magnifier or microscope
tools.why: Cracked joints and tiny parts are invisible without magnification.
how: A phone camera zoomed in works well to start.
A USB microscope or a 10× loupe is a big step up.

tools.name: Known-good cables and chargers
tools.why: To rule out the supply quickly.
how: Keep one charger and cable you know work, labelled, just for testing.
Label charge-only USB cables.

tools.name: Isopropyl alcohol (99%)
tools.why: Cleans flux, corrosion and sticky residue, and evaporates quickly.
how: Use 99% rather than 70% (which has more water).
It's flammable: use it unplugged, in a ventilated room.

tools.name: Soft brush (an old toothbrush)
tools.why: Scrubs corrosion and dust off boards.
how: Use with isopropyl alcohol.

tools.name: Soldering iron
tools.why: To replace parts and repair joints.
how: A temperature-controlled iron with a few tips (a chisel and a fine point) covers most jobs.
Keep the tip clean and tinned (coated in solder).
Work in a ventilated room.

tools.name: Solder
tools.why: Joins parts.
how: 0.5–0.8mm leaded solder (60/40 or 63/37) is the easiest to use; lead-free needs a hotter iron.
Wash your hands after handling leaded solder.

tools.name: Flux
tools.why: Makes solder flow and joints form properly.
how: A flux pen or no-clean gel flux. Clean it off afterwards with isopropyl alcohol.

tools.name: Desoldering wick or pump
tools.why: Removes solder so parts can come out.
how: Press the wick onto the joint with the iron; the solder soaks into it.
A pump sucks molten solder up in one go.

tools.name: Anti-static wrist strap
tools.why: Static from your body can damage chips.
how: Clip it to the metal of the case or an earthed point.
Work on a mat, not carpet.

tools.name: USB power meter
tools.why: Shows voltage and current through a USB cable: the quickest charging test.
how: Plug it between the charger and the device.
USB-C models also show the fast-charging protocol.

tools.name: Bench power supply
tools.why: Powers a board at a set voltage with a current limit, so a fault can't do more damage.
how: Set the voltage first, with the current limit low, before connecting.
Watch the current: a jump to the limit means a short.

tools.name: Hot-spot finder
tools.why: Finds the part that's getting hot.
how: Thermal camera: the clearest.
Isopropyl alcohol: wipe a thin film on the board; it evaporates first from the hot part.
Freeze spray: frost melts first on the hot part, and it can bring back faults that only happen when warm.
A careful fingertip works on low-voltage boards.

tools.name: Fine test probes and clips
tools.why: Reach tiny test points without slipping and shorting things.
how: Needle-point probes or grabber clips. A slipped probe can short two pins and cause damage.

tools.name: Oscilloscope
tools.why: Shows signals that change too fast for a meter: clocks, audio, data.
how: Use it to check a crystal is running, follow an audio signal, or look at ripple on a power rail.
tools.appWhy: Scopie runs USB and network scopes.

tools.name: Hot air station
tools.why: Removes and fits surface-mount parts and connectors.
how: Use plenty of flux, and protect nearby plastic parts with Kapton tape or foil.

tools.name: Heat pad or hair dryer
tools.why: Softens the glue on phones and tablets.
how: About 80°C for a few minutes, then a suction cup and picks.

tools.name: LED backlight tester
tools.why: Lights each LED in a TV backlight strip, which a meter can't.
how: Touch its probes across one LED at a time.

tools.name: Contact cleaner spray
tools.why: Cleans switches, knobs and connectors.
how: Use a cleaner made for electronics, not WD-40.

tools.name: Spare fuses
tools.why: Plug fuses (3A, 5A, 13A) and glass fuses.
how: Always replace with the same rating and type (fast or slow-blow).

tools.name: Crimp tool
tools.why: For connectors and thermal fuses that shouldn't be soldered.
how: Use the right size of crimp for the wire.

tools.name: Insulation tester or PAT tester
tools.why: Tests mains appliances at high voltage for leakage to earth.
how: A multimeter test is a rough check only: a PAT test is the proper one.

tools.name: Capacitor discharge tool
tools.why: Safely empties big capacitors in mains power supplies.
how: A 1–10kΩ resistor rated 5W or more, with insulated leads and clips. Hold it across the capacitor's legs for several seconds.
Then measure: under about 5V is safe to touch.
Never short a big capacitor with a screwdriver.

tools.name: Logic analyser
tools.why: Records several digital signals at once and decodes them: I2C, SPI, UART, keyboard scans, sync pulses.
how: Clip ground first, then one channel per signal.
Set the sample rate at least 4× the fastest signal (a 400kHz I2C bus needs 2MHz or more).
Add a decoder for the bus, then read the bytes it shows: addresses, ACK or NAK, data.
tools.appWhy: Probie runs cheap USB logic analysers, decodes the common buses and explains captures in plain words.

tools.name: Component tester or ESR meter
tools.why: Identifies and measures transistors, diodes and capacitors, and measures capacitors' ESR, which a multimeter can't.
how: Discharge capacitors before testing them.
Most testers work out an unknown part's pins for you: clip all three leads and press test.
High ESR (compared with the chart on the tester) means a dried-out capacitor even when its µF reads fine.

tools.name: Dim bulb tester
tools.why: A filament lamp in series with a mains device limits the current, so a fault can't blow parts or fuses while you test.
how: Build it only in a closed, earthed enclosure, or buy one.
Use an old-style filament bulb (40–100W), not LED.
Bright and stays bright: still a short. Flashes then dims: it starts normally.

tools.name: Signal source
tools.why: A known test tone or signal to feed into a circuit, so you can follow it through with a scope.
how: A phone's headphone output playing a 1kHz test tone (free apps) works for audio.
A cheap function generator, or a microcontroller's PWM pin, gives square waves.
Keep the level low: about 0.5V for audio inputs.

tools.name: USB-serial adapter
tools.why: Lets a computer read the debug messages many boards print at start-up, and talk to serial devices.
how: Connect its GND to the board's ground, its RX to the board's TX.
Check the board's voltage first: most need a 3.3V adapter; 5V can damage them.
Try common speeds: 115200, 9600, 57600, 74880 (ESP8266 boot messages).
tools.appWhy: Probie's Serial tab shows and explains what the board prints.

tools.name: Chip programmer
tools.why: Reads, backs up and rewrites memory chips and microcontrollers when a corrupted program is the fault.
how: Always read and save a backup before writing anything.
SPI flash chips: a CH341A programmer with a clip (check the chip's voltage: many are 1.8V or 3.3V).
Microcontrollers: the maker's programmer (ST-Link, USBasp, a Pico running debugprobe).
tools.appWhy: Flashie writes firmware to ESP32, Pico, Arduino and STM32 boards.

signs.name: Bulging or leaking capacitors
signs.look: Round electrolytic capacitors should have flat tops. Domed tops, crusty brown deposits, or a capacitor pushed up off the board mean it's failed.
signs.means: Restart loops, no power, hum, a picture that takes a while to appear.
signs.fix: Replace with the same µF, same or higher voltage, 105°C.

signs.name: Burnt parts
signs.look: Brown or black marks on the board or a part, cracked part bodies, a sharp burnt smell.
signs.means: The part failed, often because something after it shorted.
signs.fix: Replace it, and find out what made it burn.

signs.name: Corrosion
signs.look: Green, blue or white crust on contacts and pins; dull or eaten-away copper.
signs.means: Liquid got in, or a battery leaked.
signs.fix: Clean with isopropyl alcohol and a brush; replace parts that have been eaten away.

signs.name: Cracked solder joints
signs.look: A thin dark ring round a pin, or a dull, grainy joint that's lifted from the pad. Common on sockets and heavy or hot parts.
signs.means: Faults that come and go when it's moved or warms up.
signs.fix: Reflow with flux and a little fresh solder.

signs.name: A blown fuse
signs.look: Glass fuses: a broken wire inside, or blackened or silvered glass. Others: no beep on continuity.
signs.means: Too much current flowed: a surge, or a short.
signs.fix: Same rating only. If the new one blows, find the short first.

signs.name: A swollen battery
signs.look: A lithium battery that is puffy, rounded or bent instead of flat. A case or screen that is pushed apart.
signs.means: A failing battery: a fire risk.
signs.fix: Stop charging it. Remove carefully and recycle.

signs.name: Loose or damaged connectors
signs.look: A plug that wobbles, bent or missing pins, cracked joints under the socket, a ribbon cable out of its latch.
signs.means: Intermittent faults, no charging, missing picture or sound.
signs.fix: Clean, reseat, resolder, or replace the socket.

signs.name: Melted plastic
signs.look: Deformed or browned connectors, a melted plug, discoloured wire insulation.
signs.means: A poor connection or too much current made heat.
signs.fix: Replace both halves of the connector and the damaged wire.

signs.name: A broken track
signs.look: A thin crack across a copper line, often near screw holes, edges or corrosion.
signs.means: Something stopped working completely after a drop or a spill.

signs.name: Dust and hair
signs.look: Grey felt across heatsink fins, fluff round fans, hair wound round motor shafts.
signs.means: Overheating, shutdowns, a noisy or slow fan or motor.
signs.fix: Blow out with compressed air, clean the shaft.

points: Unplug it, and keep the plug where you can see it. Switching off isn't enough.
Power supplies have big capacitors that stay charged after unplugging. Wait a few minutes, then measure across them: under about 5V is safe. Use a discharge resistor if they hold charge.
On the mains side of a power supply, 'ground' is live. Never clip a probe there with it plugged in.
If you must measure with it on, keep one hand in your pocket and use probes with shrouded tips.
Never fit a bigger fuse, and never bridge a fuse with wire or foil.
After a mains repair, check the earth wire is connected and nothing bare can be touched. A PAT test is the proper check.
Disconnect the battery before anything else when you open a device.
Never puncture, bend or crush one. Use plastic tools near it.
Swollen batteries must not be charged. Store them away from anything that burns and recycle them.
Never short the terminals: big currents flow and they get very hot.
If one catches fire, get away from it and call the fire service.
The iron is about 350°C: always put it back in its stand.
Work in a ventilated room, or use a fume extractor.
Wear glasses: solder can spit.
Wash your hands after using leaded solder, and don't eat at the bench.
Touch something earthed, or wear a wrist strap, before handling boards.
Hold boards by their edges. Keep them in anti-static bags.
Isopropyl alcohol and freeze spray are flammable: use them with the device unplugged and away from the iron.
Battery leakage is caustic: wear gloves.
If you're unsure what a step involves, stop and ask, or take it to a repair shop.
If it's under warranty, opening it may void that: check first.
If parts would cost more than a replacement, a repair shop or recycling may be the better choice.
